articles.title: England v Pakistan, third men’s cricket Test, day one – live
articles.summary: Over-by-over updates from Edgbaston, 11am BST start County cricket live – follow all of today’s latest news Email Taha | And sign up to get The Spin newsletter 1st over: Pakistan 4-0 (Ayub 0, Azan 0) A welcome start for Pakistan, with leg byes travelling down the leg-side for four. Robinson, on 99 Test wickets, beats the bat with one that jags away from the left-hander … before nipping one back in for the leg-before! And up goes the finger! Ayub looked to leave and is hit well outside the line … and it’s travelling well over the stumps. Robinson must wait a little longer for No 100. The anthems have wrapped up. Time for Ollie Robinson to wobble the ball down. Saim Ayub is on strike. Continue reading...
articles.content:
12th over: Pakistan 35-4 (Babar 2, Shakeel 5) Babar played a cracking knock against New Zealand on this ground seven years ago in the World Cup, hitting an unbeaten ton in a successful chase of 238. Happier days. Gus Atkinson whizzes the ball past Babar’s outside edge on the way to a maiden.

11th over: Pakistan 35-4 (Babar 2, Shakeel 5) Robinson slides down the leg side and Smith, up to the stumps, isn’t getting that. It runs away for four byes. The catch off Masood was taken by Theo Wylie, by the way, a 20-year-old at Warwickshire.

10th over: Pakistan 29-4 (Babar 2, Shakeel 3) Saud Shakeel, so close to a ton at Lord’s, punches through mid-off for three. We’re one wicket away from the keeper on debut. Babar, bounced out by Archer in London, flashes outside off and only catches air.

Ollie Robinson’s Test bowling average has dropped to 19.19. Ridiculous, isn’t it? And now another for Archer – a truly horrid dismissal. Masood falls like Azan, awkwardly shoving the ball into the leg-side, chipping it for the easiest of grabs at midwicket. This has been a horrible, horrible first hour for Pakistan. And it’s not a surprise.

9th over: Pakistan 26-3 (Babar 2, Masood 5) Five men make up England’s slip cordon … but Babar Azam clips into the leg-side for a couple.

And another. Robinson’s relentlessness tells, finding the outside edge of Shafique, and Dan Lawrence cleans up in the stacked cordon. This one-sided series refuses to change its rhythm.

8th over: Pakistan 24-2 (Shafique 3, Masood 5) Archer finds Masood’s outside edge … but the ball finds the gap in the cordon to run away for four.

7th over: Pakistan 18-2 (Shafique 2, Masood 0) Masood is playing his 50th Test – it’s taken him 13 years to get there. Robinson continues to toy with Shafique, the ball constantly threatening to brush the outside edge.

6th over: Pakistan 16-2 (Shafique 0, Masood 0) Shan Masood is hit first ball on the pad … it looks close to me but England aren’t going to review. Maybe sliding down leg.

Dropped! Azan – unable to score off Robinson – drives loosely at Archer, and an edge carries low to Ben Duckett at first slip … but he can’t gobble it up. Not that it really matters: Azan is left in a tangle on the back foot and chips to Josh Tongue at midwicket. Oh dear.

5th over: Pakistan 13-1 (Shafique 0, Azan 9) Robinson looks dangerous with every ball, refusing to miss his spot. Azan, covering his stumps, can’t do anything about another delivery that jags extravagantly away from his bat.

4th over: Pakistan 13-1 (Shafique 0, Azan 9) Azan looks confident, driving Archer through the covers again for his second boundary. Archer then pulls back his length to jag the ball away from the southpaw.

3rd over: Pakistan 8-1 (Shafique 0, Azan 4) Abdullah Shafique is in at three for Pakistan, with Shan Masood dropping to four. Jamie Smith is up to the stumps … as Robinson bowls a corker, nipping it away from the right-hander. It’s a fine take from the keeper, too.

Ayub is given out again! And he reviews once more … but this looks fairly plumb to me. Robinson wobbles it into the left-hander and slaps the back pad. It’s smashing into leg stump and that is a really poor review. It’s a 10-ball duck for the recalled opener. Robinson has his 100th Test wicket!

2nd over: Pakistan 8-0 (Ayub 0, Azan 4) Jofra Archer has two left-handers to play with as Azan, who battled hard at Lord’s, unfurls a lush drive through the covers to close the over, punishing a half volley.

1st over: Pakistan 4-0 (Ayub 0, Azan 0) A welcome start for Pakistan, with leg byes travelling down the leg-side for four. Robinson, on 99 Test wickets, beats the bat with one that jags away from the left-hander … before nipping one back in for the leg-before! And up goes the finger! Ayub looked to leave and is hit well outside the line … and it’s travelling well over the stumps. Robinson must wait a little longer for No 100.

The anthems have wrapped up. Time for Ollie Robinson to wobble the ball down. Saim Ayub is on strike.

Winning this match would be maximum Pakistan ridiculousness. And who knows? England have a long history of ridiculousness too.

Saim Ayub has flown in from the Caribbean Premier League … to take on a new-ball duo of Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer. Ayub hasn’t played a first-class match since last October, hasn’t played a Test since January 2025. He’ll probably have to play a role with the ball, too, as Pakistan’s only spin option. Good luck to him.

Pakistan have three debutants and make four changes to the XI that played at Lord’s. Saim Ayub slots in at the top of the order and there are caps for Ghazi Ghori, Razaullah and Mohammad Imran.

England: Emilio Gay, Ben Duckett, Jordan Cox, Joe Root (c), Harry Brook, Dan Lawrence, Jamie Smith (wk), Gus Atkinson, Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue

Pakistan: Azan Awais, Saim Ayub, Abdullah Shafique, Shan Masood, Babar Azam (c), Saud Shakeel, Ghazi Ghori (wk), Mohammad Imran, Razaullah, Mohammad Ali, Mohammad Abbas

Joe Root says he likes the overheads. England aren’t messing about – they’re unchanged.

The County Championship roars on. Tanya’s keeping tabs from Old Trafford.

There are some chilly white-ball games still to come this month and with it the sight of Kevin Pietersen back in England training kit for the first time in 12 years. KP is down with the kids these days, 6/7 memes and the like , and starts a new life as the “specialist mentor” to Harry Brook’s young thrusters.

But the final Test of the summer that starts at Edgbaston on Wednesday does feel like an end of sorts, or at least one last push before a breather for the side that has undergone the more significant recalibration. And that is before we get on to Pakistan and a tour that has descended into a bonfire of players and a phone-snatching investigation into “discipline and conduct” .

Hello, hello, hello and welcome to the last Test of the English summer. It’s been a wild one: beginning with Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum, ending with Joe Root and Marcus Trescothick. Stephen Fleming’s on the way. There’s been late-night drama, a series defeat to New Zealand, and a comfortable triumph against Pakistan. But the hosts aren’t the story today. No, it’s all Pakistan, with their board’s frankly ridiculous decision to discard seven players and two coaches after the second Test at Lord’s. A remarkable toss awaits as Babar Azam is asked about any changes to his XI. This bizarre dead rubber gets going at 11am BST.

articles.title: Petrol prices rise by 5p over a week as Iran war sends oil higher
articles.summary: A litre of unleaded now costs 167.17p which is the biggest weekly increase since April, data shows.
articles.content:
The average price of unleaded petrol has risen by 5p a litre in the space of a week, according to the RAC, which warned there was "no sign of any relief" for drivers.

The motoring organisation said a litre of unleaded now costs 167.17p - the biggest weekly increase since April - while diesel has also risen by 5p to 188.63p.

Fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel - across the Middle East.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, has returned to $100 a barrel, for the first time since July, as hostilities escalated again.

US forces struck five Iranian tankers after Tehran targeted one of its warships, while Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement also attacked oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

The price of Brent is some way off the $120 it hit in April, but remains well above the $70 it was trading at before the conflict started.

RAC senior policy officer Rod Dennis said the latest increase in fuel prices showed just how exposed drivers in the UK can be to events thousands of miles away.

The 5p a litre rise meant the cost of filling a family-sized car had increased by £2.75 over the past week, he added.

"Drivers are having to dig ever deeper into their pockets every time they fill up, and there's no sign of any relief yet," said Dennis.

"With the cost of a barrel of oil having averaged $96 for the last week, wholesale prices are surging and that's already feeding through to prices at the forecourt."

He urged motorists to drive as efficiently as possible and to ensure they find the cheapest forecourts they can.

The last time petrol was this high was in September 2022, while diesel is still a bit below the 191.54p it reached in April.

Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes

articles.title: Leicestershire v Somerset, Nottinghamshire v Hampshire, and more: county cricket, day two – live
articles.summary: County Championship updates as the title race heats up Mail Tanya or post BTL | Sign up for The Spin newsletter Unfortunately it wasn’t a rubicon that Crawley crossed with that eighty the other week, Ben Aitchisoned for 6. Kent 22-2, surely they won’t let it slip out of their grasp now? Sussex won the toss at Hove and bat first, perhaps not wanting to risk Surrey’s Indian left-arm spinner Mahipal Lomror batting fourth. They’ve nudged along to 16-0. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Langridge, headband, under lights, runs in from the Brian Statham end. Three slips, hands on knees wait.

With an hour gone, time to wander around the grounds. In Division Two:

Kent are wobbling, 67-3, but young Bertie Foreman is still there on 33. Sam Northeast out cheaply. Kent trail Derby by 232.

A super catch by Jennings at slip gives Stanley a second wicket and bowls out Gloucestershire for 212.

Middlesex are holding up against Durham , 118-3, trail by 134, Holden last out for 43. Two wickets for Carse.

And Taylor and Finch have made early inroads into Northants , 63-2 after Worcs were all out for 200.

A maiden fifty for Daz Ahmed in his sixth f-c match. A nice round of applause from the fleeced-up OT crowd. Glos 197-8.

Leicestershire 37-2, both to one-man-brass-band Lewis Gregory. I’d really love to see Rehan Ahmed (16) make a century here. He was so so good last year, my favourite player to watch.

Sonny Baker will stay with the Test team for the next couple of days before joining up with the Lions on Friday.

“Morning, Tanya.” Good morning Max Bonnell! ( I loved Father Marriot’s Summer Holiday by the way, such a good read).

“Serious question: only a few seasons back Lancashire was pressing for the Division One title. How have they managed to become so bad at cricket, so quickly?”

That’s a question! In short: injuries, loss of form for senior pros, loss of confidence, strange management, odd signings, bad luck. For more details, see BTL!

Anderson at slip leaps like a lampost and holds on, giving Mitch Stanley his first wicket of the innings. Williams trudges away for four, Gloucs 183-8.

James Rew was last man out for Somerset (61); Sheridon Gumbs is first man out for Leicestershire (0). Leics 5-1.

Unfortunately it wasn’t a rubicon that Crawley crossed with that eighty the other week, Ben Aitchisoned for 6. Kent 22-2, surely they won’t let it slip out of their grasp now?

Sussex won the toss at Hove and bat first, perhaps not wanting to risk Surrey’s Indian left-arm spinner Mahipal Lomror batting fourth. They’ve nudged along to 16-0.

We’ve just been pondering the strange career of Tom Hartley, who didn’t play for his Hundred franchise, isn’t wanted in the Championship side, but is now playing for the England Lions. I hope he finds his way. And that’s a fourth wicket for the hard-working Balderson, Kishore bowled for 20. Gloucs 171-7.

Noman Ali gets one over this morning, after not bowling at all at Merchant Taylor’s and barely bowling at Worcester.

A good scattering of people in at OT for a dead match in September. From the Jimmy Anderson end, JimmyAnderson.

And the unstoppable Kyle Abbott, after Notts got away from Hampshire at Trent Bridge.

“When you win the toss and bowl on that pitch with lights on, you frankly should do better. We were quite far off mark and I’m pretty disappointed to be honest.

“It was the most grass I’ve seen on a pitch in quite some while. But we’d kind of expected it, I suppose. Notts are champions and at the top while we’ve not had a great summer so they have the right, really. The par for that pitch was probably between 160 and 180, maybe 200 once the ball got softer.

“Amongst it all in a disappointing season I’ve enjoyed it because of the younger boys. We are not short of effort or commitment and the skills should come. I’m trying to help as much as I can with that.”

Ethan Bamber, whose five wickets ripped through Glamorgan’s top order as they were bowled out for 69, spoke last night:

“I got a good amount of good fortune. The pitch seamed a bit, I think just repeat good balls actually I was lucky to return those figures, I didn’t bowl my best at all. There was a lot down leg-side, a lot of half-volleys and a wicket off a no ball but there was enough good stuff in between.

“It’s a slow wicket and on those surfaces you get a bit of moisture then they dry out and we’re lucky they did a bit early on and it’ll get easier.”

Here’s Ali’s preview of the final Test of the summer, starting at Edgbaston at 11 (I wonder why they don’t start at 10.30?)

The three leading contenders for the Division One title, Somerset, Warwickshire and Nottinghamshire , each had a profitable day, though Warwickshire swung the biggest hammer after dismissing Glamorgan for 69 at Sophia Gardens.

Ethan Bamber was chief destroyer, with five for 28, passing 50 wickets for the season, while Ed Barnard (three for five) provided able backup. There were no demons in the dirt for the visitors, who eased to 154 for three.

Joe Clarke hit his fourth Championship century of the season to rescue Nottinghamshire from the doldrums of 20 for three as Hampshire ’s Kyle Abbott made the most of a bile-coloured pitch. Liam Patterson-White (92) and the tail then sailed Notts past 350. Felix Organ and Nick Gubbins survived four overs of evening torment from Olly Stone and Dillon Pennington.

Somerset arrived at Grace Road to find the mood music gloomy after Leicestershire were charged with breaching pitch regulations during their match against Glamorgan in August. Leicestershire “strongly dispute the allegations”, but risk losing the 19 points from that game if the Cricket Discipline Panel finds against them, a kick in the teeth to their hopes of staying in Division One.

Spirits will not have been any brighter when Somerset’s Josh Thomas and Tom Lammonby added 181 for the first wicket. Thomas, just 21 pocketed his third hundred of the year.

Derbyshire fought back from nought for two after two balls against Kent , thanks to an undefeated 129 from Martin Andersson and 47 extras. Bangladesh pace bowler Hasan Mahmud grabbed four wickets. Promotion chasing Kent had four overs to bat and Ben Compton was inevitably [Ben] Aitchisoned.

George Balderson, three for 35 and a run out, had a good day out against Gloucestershire at Old Trafford; while Essex had the best – just – of a relegation rumble against Yorkshire , who lost five for 18 after a prosperous morning.

Good morning from an autumnal Manchester, heavy dew, overgrown hydrangeas and a dash of sun. After yesterday’s rain, today looks more promising as the top three jostle for position. We’ll be here all day, do join us.

“I got a good amount of good fortune. The pitch seamed a bit, I think just repeat good balls actually I was lucky to return those figures, I didn’t bowl my best at all. There was a lot down leg-side, a lot of half-volleys and a wicket off a no ball but there was enough good stuff in between.
“It’s a slow wicket and on those surfaces you get a bit of moisture then they dry out and we’re lucky they did a bit early on and it’ll get easier.”
Here’s Ali’s preview of the final Test of the summer, starting at Edgbaston at 11 (I wonder why they don’t start at 10.30?)

The three leading contenders for the Division One title, Somerset, Warwickshire and Nottinghamshire , each had a profitable day, though Warwickshire swung the biggest hammer after dismissing Glamorgan for 69 at Sophia Gardens.

Ethan Bamber was chief destroyer, with five for 28, passing 50 wickets for the season, while Ed Barnard (three for five) provided able backup. There were no demons in the dirt for the visitors, who eased to 154 for three.

Joe Clarke hit his fourth Championship century of the season to rescue Nottinghamshire from the doldrums of 20 for three as Hampshire ’s Kyle Abbott made the most of a bile-coloured pitch. Liam Patterson-White (92) and the tail then sailed Notts past 350. Felix Organ and Nick Gubbins survived four overs of evening torment from Olly Stone and Dillon Pennington.

Somerset arrived at Grace Road to find the mood music gloomy after Leicestershire were charged with breaching pitch regulations during their match against Glamorgan in August. Leicestershire “strongly dispute the allegations”, but risk losing the 19 points from that game if the Cricket Discipline Panel finds against them, a kick in the teeth to their hopes of staying in Division One.
Spirits will not have been any brighter when Somerset’s Josh Thomas and Tom Lammonby added 181 for the first wicket. Thomas, just 21 pocketed his third hundred of the year.

Derbyshire fought back from nought for two after two balls against Kent , thanks to an undefeated 129 from Martin Andersson and 47 extras. Bangladesh pace bowler Hasan Mahmud grabbed four wickets. Promotion chasing Kent had four overs to bat and Ben Compton was inevitably [Ben] Aitchisoned.

George Balderson, three for 35 and a run out, had a good day out against Gloucestershire at Old Trafford; while Essex had the best – just – of a relegation rumble against Yorkshire , who lost five for 18 after a prosperous morning.

Good morning from an autumnal Manchester, heavy dew, overgrown hydrangeas and a dash of sun. After yesterday’s rain, today looks more promising as the top three jostle for position. We’ll be here all day, do join us.

articles.content:
CEOs may like to get up at the crack of dawn and go for a run, but I prefer optimising my life with lie-ins, trashy films, swearing and coffee

T his evening I’m going to tuck my five-year-old into bed and read her a chapter from one of her princess books, followed by a summary of research recently presented at the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology. Once upon a time, I’ll tell her, there was a scientist called Dr Nawon Lee who authored a study that found having a weekend lie-in may be very good for you and can protect against high blood pressure. Our accomplished protagonist Dr Lee said: “People should not feel lazy or guilty for sleeping a little longer on the weekend.” And the moral of this story, dear child, is that you should try not to wake your mothers up at 6am every day.

Unfortunately, I’m not sure that all the peer-reviewed science in the world will convince my early riser to have a weekend lie-in. Still, as a big fan of sleep and someone who has never once felt guilty for hitting the snooze button, I have to say I feel vindicated by this new study. CEOs can get up at 4am and run 10 miles before eating five foraged mushrooms if they want to, but I’m going to protect my heart health by sleeping in, any opportunity I can get, thank you very much.

The rich world is currently in thrall to tech-enabled self-optimisation. Or as some people (people you do not want to end up seated next to at a dinner party) call it: humanmaxxing . We’re told we should track our biomarkers and optimise every second of our days, often in complicated and joyless ways. If that works for you, great. But, personally, I’m a big fan of lazymaxxing and finding low-effort ways to improve my life. Weekend lie-ins are obviously one, drinking coffee is another. A 2025 study found that morning coffee drinkers were 16% less likely to die early of any cause. Swearing is also surprisingly good for you : uttering a profanity can decrease physical pain and increase focus. And while I can’t go so far as to say that bingeing Love is Blind has health-giving properties, I did unearth research concluding that enjoying trashy films is a sign you’re a well-educated cultural omnivore. I still haven’t found a study proving that lying on the couch, eating crisps, reading thrillers and ignoring your obligations is good for you, but I live in hope.

articles.title: England to extend Borthwick contract as Pollock closes on £400,000 Northampton deal
articles.summary: RFU eager to avoid uncertainty heading into World Cup Lloyds Bank to pay £5m a year for logo on back of jerseys Steve Borthwick will be handed a contract extension until after the 2028 Six Nations, giving the Rugby Football Union time to identify his successor if England flop at the World Cup next year. The RFU’s move is designed to avoid uncertainty heading into the tournament but stops short of backing Borthwick in the long term. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Steve Borthwick will be handed a contract extension until after the 2028 Six Nations, giving the Rugby Football Union time to identify his successor if England flop at the World Cup next year.

The RFU’s move is designed to avoid uncertainty heading into the tournament but stops short of backing Borthwick in the long term.

Borthwick is contracted until the end of the tournament next year and the RFU’s director of performance, Conor O’Shea, has made clear that his future beyond that is dependent on how England perform in Australia.

The head coach came out of England’s worst Six Nations campaign this year under considerable pressure but the RFU chief executive, Bill Sweeney, has given his backing for Borthwick to lead the side into the tournament next year.

“You don’t want them looking for a job going into [a World Cup],” O’Shea said. “Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can’t have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing. So we will give that certainty, and that will give us time to look properly.”

O’Shea has made clear that Borthwick must target World Cup glory in Australia and, while Andy Farrell has been handed a contract with Ireland through to 2031 the RFU has not presented Borthwick with similar long-term backing.

England were thrashed by South Africa at the start of their summer tour before a comfortable victory against Fiji and a narrow win against Argentina. Borthwick’s job will come under further pressure if England disappoint in autumn fixtures against Australia, Japan, New Zealand as well as a final weekend rankings match.

“I see in Steve someone who bleeds England and wants England to succeed more than anything you can imagine,” O’Shea said. “This England team is unequivocally one of probably five teams who can win the World Cup next year. I believe this team can win a World Cup. Is the talent there? One hundred per cent. If over this next 12 months this England team shows the best version of itself, I know it can beat anyone in the world.”

The RFU, meanwhile, has announced a new money-spinning venture with England jerseys to have a sponsor emblazoned across the back for the first time. The deal with Lloyds Bank is thought to be worth £5m a year, with Sweeney claiming the arrangement gives the union “largest sponsorship revenue in world rugby”.

The Guardian revealed the RFU was on the verge of confirming the deal as the latest in a string of new sponsorships. England jerseys will feature the Lloyds logo during the Nations Championship this autumn and brings the RFU in line with rivals such as France, who have a similar arrangement with Société Générale. Under tournament rules, England will not be permitted to have sponsorship logos on jerseys during the World Cup next year, however.

As part of the multi-year deal the Lloyds black horse will feature on the jerseys of the men’s and women’s teams as well as the training jackets. The jerseys will continue to feature the O2 logo on the front while the RFU secured a kit deal with Castore in 2025.

The RFU is attempting to diversify revenue streams, with the Guardian revealing that the union is expecting to post a £10m loss for the financial year ending 2026 compared with £2m the previous year. The union has told its member clubs that England’s dismal performance in the Six Nations was a contributing factor to the forecasted eight-figure loss.

The year ending 2027 is expected to be more prosperous with sponsorship revenues playing a key factor but the year ending 2028 will incur heavy losses because of the World Cup and the absence of autumn internationals at Twickenham.

Meanwhile, Henry Pollock is nearing a new deal with Northampton believed to be worth more than £400,000, ending speculation over the England flanker’s future. The 21-year-old’s agent, Eddie Hearn, had claimed Pollock should be earning £1m a year but the Northampton director of rugby, Phil Dowson, insisted last week that a “happy medium” must be reached.

Pollock is poised to roughly triple his salary without Northampton having to break the bank to keep the star player, who has 13 England caps to his name.

articles.content:
From face tints and self-tan to summer scents, these lightweight buys saw me through multiple heatwaves

Y ou’ll normally find me looking back on my favourite products of the past 12 months at year’s end. But this summer has been so freakishly hot and sweaty it has required its own toolkit and, by extension, its own list of exceptionally well-performing products that deserve rapturous commendation.

The first is Refy’s Skin Base (£30), a sheer face tint so thin and so lightweight it has been all I could bear to wear since July. It’s suitable for all skin types, but not at all appropriate for those who hate any hint of shine. While the texture is totally ungreasy, breathable and so comfortable as to be imperceptible, it does look unmistakably dewy, so avoid if you’re devoted to matte. Personally, I take the view that, in this heat, one might as well steer into the skid, but I am, admittedly, at an age when a juicier look works in my skin’s favour. Anyway, this is makeup that truly feels like absolutely nothing, and what it lacks in coverage can be made up with concealer where needed. Maximum points from me (I wear shade 140N).

Moisturiser is another step that humidity has forced me to downsize. The heat has made wearing heavy face cream as appealing as a 5km parkrun, so I’ve switched to lighter liquids to quench my skin’s thirst. The Prequel skincare line, which recently launched in the UK, is consistently good, but its Half & Half Fluid Moisturi zer (£28) has been a godsend. This very lightweight emulsion pours like semi-skimmed milk, satisfies like double cream and barely adds any weight to sweaty skin. The glycerin and ceramides keep everything supple until bedtime, and give a smooth, plump base for SPF and makeup. It’s the skincare equivalent of sleeping underneath a silk sheet instead of a 9-tog duvet.

St Tropez’s new Instant Glow Mousse (£25) has never been far from my reach. It’s a fast, mess-free and streakless way to make exposed legs golden until your next soapy shower. Stroke on with a mitt, wash off only when you’re ready. Absolutely no fussy prep required.

I’ve relied heavily on zingy, fresh, enlivening scents to keep me in good spirits. The summer 2026 perfume playlist I’ve had on repeat is Dedcool’s Xtra Milk (from £24) – a dreadful name, but a very gentle, happy and wearable fragrance – and Penhaligon’s Luna (from £32), all wet roses, zesty citrus and airy green forests. Like a cold compress for the senses.

articles.title: An embattled Donald Trump is increasingly using sports as prop | Leander Schaerlaeckens
articles.summary: Sports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms Lately, it seems Donald Trump’s scope of interests has narrowed to a few things: remaking downtown Washington DC in his gaudy image; wars he thinks he can win quickly and easily, even though he can’t. Also, golf. Always golf. Ever golf. Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now . He teaches at Marist University. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Sports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms

L ately, it seems Donald Trump’s scope of interests has narrowed to a few things: remaking downtown Washington DC in his gaudy image; wars he thinks he can win quickly and easily, even though he can’t.

We hear less and less about Trump’s plans to overhaul healthcare, reshore manufacturing jobs or address the budget deficit. Yet one other subject, aligned with his lifelong interests, continues to preoccupy him: sports.

And in this area, his ideological project has methodically and loudly – since nothing of consequence can ever be done quietly by this administration – made more gains than just about anywhere else.

Which is to say that Trump, or more likely those seeking to swim in the slipstream of Trumpism , are hard at work trying to put sports back to how it looked in the 1980s. After all, that’s when the president’s view of the world, and how it should function, ossified.

This manifests in ways big and small, in consequences intended and accidental.

Here’s a relatively small and surely accidental one. When Los Angeles FC sold Venezuela international David Martínez to Denmark’s FC Midtjylland for $8.4m recently, the club did not do so for sporting reasons – or not entirely. The winger, named to the Guardian’s 2023 Next Generation class, had difficulty adapting to life in Los Angeles after arriving as an 18-year-old because his family couldn’t get visas to visit him, according to the club.

If Trump and his goons had even heard of the now-20-year-old, which they almost certainly hadn’t, he would have hardly been a top target of their policies. But that they have driven him to leave the country will would satisfy them all the same. This is exactly what the administration’s travel bans and curbs on visas were intended to achieve: to put people off coming to the US, or staying here.

The rolling campaign to “save” women’s sports from transgender athletes, who exist in vanishingly small numbers and are far from the threat those on the right would have you believe. This panic is propagated by a rabble who very proudly didn’t care about women’s sports at all until they spotted an opening to make a political profit from it.

Trump’s looming presence over the summer’s World Cup, and his active interference in it. His attendance at the NBA finals, the Daytona 500 and the Ryder Cup, appearances that seemed to curse his favored participants.

There’s the executive order attempting to unwind the decades-overdue gains made by college athletes in winning the right to be treated like every other American worker. They can finally be paid for their valuable labor and move (almost) freely between programs in search of the best opportunities – same as their coaches and administrators have always been able to do.

Foreign students and college athletes, meanwhile, find it harder and less attractive to come to and stay in the US on account of the same difficulties in bagging visas that chased off Martínez. That makes college sports more homogeneous and therefore, in Trump’s thinking, better.

The College Football Playoff’s lurching expansion threatened to creep into the second Saturday of December, traditionally and legally set aside for the Commander-in-Chief’s Trophy.

“Such scheduling conflicts weaken the national focus on our Military Service Academies and detract from a morale-building event of vital interest to the Department of War,” the order reads.

Also apparently intended as a morale-building event was the much-panned UFC event on the White House lawn to celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary, and, more pressingly, Trump’s 80th birthday. The first professional sporting event on the White House grounds managed to lose $30m , even though the fighters were apparently paid at least partly in cryptocurrency issued by a Trump company.

When he sensed he would be met by a friendly crowd, Trump became the first sitting president to attend the Super Bowl . In the same spirit, he traveled to a World Series game in 2021, when he was out of power, just to do the racist tomahawk chop with Atlanta Braves fans.

He more or less ordered an IndyCar race to be held in DC, the Freedom 250, which was well attended but severely disrupted car and plane traffic in the capital. The awkward layout of the course, meanwhile, meant that nearly half the cars didn’t finish all the laps. No matter, Trump took a lap around the track in his presidential limousine. With no other cars on the road, he finished first.

Then there are the unprovoked and untethered broadsides. Such as the time Trump suggested the National Football League change its name to accommodate soccer. Or suggested LeBron James was a racist because he doesn’t play golf with the president. Or when he plunged a cleaver into the culture war prime cuts of restoring the Washington Commanders and Cleveland Guardians to their old, racist names.

Yet the lesson that has stuck with him since childhood is that sports holds a privileged place in our national conscience, and that it serves as a powerful messaging conduit. Now, as president, his efforts have hardly been concerted or coordinated, but sports is the rare topic where Trump has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now . He teaches at Marist University.

articles.title: Revitalised Ødegaard’s forward thinking gives Arsenal new lines of attack
articles.summary: Midfielder has been pivotal to the champions’ rampant start, becoming a potent threat with his runs into the box As Christos Tzolis cut in from the left flank and drove towards the penalty area, Kai Havertz could see history repeating itself. Tzolis had done just the same on his competitive debut for Arsenal against Manchester City in the Community Shield a few weeks earlier, running at his opposition full-back, cutting inside and driving at goal, before fizzing a ball towards the penalty spot. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Midfielder has been pivotal to the champions’ rampant start, becoming a potent threat with his runs into the box

As Christos Tzolis cut in from the left flank and drove towards the penalty area, Kai Havertz could see history repeating itself.

Tzolis had done just the same on his competitive debut for Arsenal against Manchester City in the Community Shield a few weeks earlier, running at his opposition full-back, cutting inside and driving at goal, before fizzing a ball towards the penalty spot.

Martin Ødegaard was the grateful recipient, arriving just behind Havertz to take the ball smoothly into his path. He then faked a shot to send Gianluigi Donnarumma the wrong way before passing into the empty net.

With the scores level early in the second half of Arsenal’s win against Chelsea on Sunday, Tzolis did something very similar.

This time, his pass was intended for Havertz, but it was played ever so slightly behind the German. But Havertz had watched this before. He knew that Ødegaard, upon seeing Tzolis cut in, would have tiptoed into the penalty area.

Havertz produced a moment of genius to turn Tzolis’s slightly misplaced pass into a perfect assist, lifting his foot over the ball to leave it for his captain. Ødegaard again took the ball under his control with one touch, before this time lifting it over Emiliano Martínez to put Arsenal into a lead they would not surrender .

Ødegaard getting into more advanced positions has been an early theme of this season. He has three goals in four appearances, after scoring once in 36 outings last season.

There has clearly been an effort from Mikel Arteta and his staff to get their fit-again midfielder into attacking areas more consistently. In Premier League games this season, Ødegaard is making 3.2 high-intensity runs per 90 minutes into the opposition’s box while Arsenal have possession, up from 1.4 per 90 last term.

It’s only a small sample size from this season, but the fact that his numbers have more than doubled makes it significant nonetheless. And most important, his goal threat has clearly skyrocketed.

Similarly, he has made seven off-ball runs to make himself a cross option for a teammate in three Premier League games, almost matching his tally from last season (10). On a per-90 basis, that’s 0.65 to 2.8, or more than a fourfold increase. One of those runs led to his goal in the season opener against Coventry .

After an injury-disrupted couple of years, it appears the far-from-linear rise of the 27-year-old has taken a steep, upward turn for the better. And, for an Arsenal team looking imperious this season, that is a very positive sign.

Their captain played his part in their 2025-26 title triumph, but he probably feels more driven than most at the club to repeat the trick. He missed a big chunk of the season with a series of recurring knee injuries, and when he was available he was used sparingly.

He played 1,371 of a possible 3,420 minutes in the league – a scratch over 40.0% – and although he was available for the run-in, playing in key games and in Arsenal’s run to the Champions League final, he was a long way from the key man he has been since his permanent move to the club in the summer of 2021.

Back then Arsenal were signing a hugely talented No 10, but Ødegaard has developed into more of a No 8, a rounded midfielder who drops deep to get on the ball in front of the opposition’s midfield and moves it around the pitch.

The evidence this season suggests that we should expect to see him getting closer to Havertz more often (while also continuing to do the job of a No 8). Havertz isn’t the most reliable goalscorer, but he is an excellent and intelligent centre-forward who performs more of a false 9 role, and he needs more runners ahead of him than Viktor Gyökeres.

It appears this season that Arteta is going to prefer using Havertz up front, which will increase the need for Ødegaard to score more consistently. After the Norwegian’s start, he should at the very least challenge his season-best 15 goals in all competitions from 2022-23. He is averaging 5.6 high-intensity runs ahead of the ball per 90 this season, up from 3.9 last term.

He seems to have benefited from this summer’s World Cup, where he played a key role in his team’s run to the quarter-finals. Only Michael Olise (seven) got more assists at the tournament than Ødegaard (four).

There is pressure on him at club level, though. Eberechi Eze is breathing down his neck after standing in for him for large swathes of last season, though Arteta clearly prefers Ødegaard in the middle, perhaps for his defensive work, positioning and ability to coach Arsenal’s press on the pitch.

But there is just as much pressure on him to stay fit. He started 32, 37 and 35 of a possible 38 Premier League games in his first three full seasons, but has managed 26 then 16 in the past two.

He needs to prove he can stay fit, because not only are Arsenal better with him, but he is more likely to maintain his best form that way.

Ødegaard is showing his best in the early part of 2026-27. He is, along with Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers, one of only two players with at least 1.0 expected goals and 1.0 expected assists in the Premier League, highlighting his all-round attacking game.

Only seven players have played a role in more open-play shot-ending sequences than him (20), and he leads the Premier League for the number of such sequences where he took the shot and was involved in the buildup (four).

It helps that Arsenal look a very functional team, and have benefited from limited changes in personnel over the summer. But how much is that functionality a cause of Ødegaard’s form and how much is it a result? During his time at the club Arsenal have mounted sustained challenges for the Premier League title, and that is surely no coincidence.

Ødegaard is looking back to his best and then some, and that is ominous news for the rest of the Premier League.

articles.title: US Open 2026 quarter-final: Ben Shelton stuns Carlos Alcaraz in thriller after latest ever finish – as it happened
articles.summary: Shelton sees off Alcaraz in latest ever US Open finish Tiafoe breaks Michelsen’s heart with epic comeback First set: Shelton 3-2 Alcaraz* (*denotes next server) An even breezier service game from Shelton, who holds to love. During the changeover, the cameras pan to a few of the celebrities in the audience. There’s Kevin Hart taking it in from a suite. And, of course, there’s USA and Washington Spirit forward Trinity Rodman, Shelton’s girlfriend, watching from his player box. We’ve also heard Simone Biles is in the building somewhere. Continue reading...
articles.content:
And Shelton has done it, closing it out with a 146mph out wide. Carlos Alcaraz is out of the US Open and Ben Shelton will meet Frances Tiafoe in an all-American semi-final on Friday!

That’s all for tonight. Er, this morning. Thanks for following along with us and be sure to read Tumaini Carayol’s full report off a match for the record books.

Shelton also spoke warmly about the communication with his father and coach, Bryan, during a match that stretched deep into the New York night. “For us, it was just enjoyable to be a part of that match,” he says. “Obviously, the level of tennis, how long the match was going, the fight that it was, how even the match was back and forth throughout. I think that’s something that we can appreciate. Win or lose, have a smile on our face.”

And after nearly four and a half hours on court, is he worried about recovering in time for Friday’s semi-final with Frances Tiafoe ? Shelton’s answer at 3.46am on Wednesday morning was to the point. “Two days? Yeah.”

Shelton admits he was “pissed” after losing that 70-minute opening set , particularly after breaking Alcaraz to force the tiebreak. But that late break also gave him belief. “I knew that my serve was only going to get better, and if I’d already dialed in the return to the point that I could break him, I thought my chances were good to get that second set.”

That proved prescient. Shelton broke Alcaraz three times in a runaway second set, and from there felt able to “play and swing more freely”. The key, he says, was staying patient on return: making Alcaraz play, punishing missed spots and not getting discouraged by the inevitable aces and service winners. “I think for me to be able to hang in there in the rallies, have a game plan from the ground and be able to execute that game plan, and not be losing all the baseline points, also helps with the return.”

How does Ben Shelton feel after Tuesday night’s/Wednesday morning’s quarter-final win? “I’m tired,” the American said to a gaggle of reporters in the bowels of Arthur Ashe Stadium, in lieu of a formal press conference given the late hour.

“That was a war, epic match. I mean, so physical. Carlos, one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old. It’s always fun being on the court against him. It’s ridiculous, the amount of stuff he comes up with sometimes, but the most enjoyable match that I’ve had in my career, for sure.”

What an ending. After 4hr 28min, Shelton finally gets over the line in a fifth-set tiebreak to reach the US Open semi-finals, surviving Alcaraz’s furious fourth-set comeback and a deciding set in which neither man could find the break.

The serve that carried Shelton for so much of the night held firm when it mattered most. He won 70% of his first-serve points and 57% behind his second serve, with 54 of his 156 serves going unreturned. Remarkably, after Alcaraz broke him three times in that fourth-set rout, Shelton did not surrender serve in the decider.

And the contrast in errors tells plenty of the story. Alcaraz finished with 38 winners to Shelton’s 34, but committed 53 unforced errors to the American’s 35. Shelton also dominated the short exchanges, winning 55% of rallies lasting four shots or fewer, while Alcaraz controlled the longer ones. In the end, at nearly four and a half hours and deep into the New York night, the margins could scarcely have been finer.

Shelton pounds a 146mph serve that Alcaraz can’t handle. Then Alcaraz makes another unforced error off the forehand side to go down a minibreak! He wins the next point coming to net with a drop-shot volley winner. But Shelton is serving for the match at 8-7 with the next two points on his racket.

Alcaraz makes an unforced error from the baseline and we’re back on serve in the breaker. He then fires in an unreturnable serve. Shelton to serve at 5-6. That beeping you may hear is the sound of the garbage trucks. What an atmosphere. Shelton wins the next point for 6-all and the players will change ends again. The end is near.

Alcaraz crushes a picture-perfect winner into the corner and now Shelton will serve at 3-4 with the next two points on his racket. An unforced error on Shelton’s forehand gives Alcaraz a minibreak, but the American wins the next point with a body serve that Alcaraz can’t handle. Alcaraz to serve at 5-4.

Shelton wins the next point but then falters on a backhand, handing the minibreak back to Alcaraz. On serve in the tiebreaker. Another unforced error by Shelton makes it 3-all as the players change ends.

Shelton serves to begin the tiebreak and rips a forehand winner early in the rally. Alcaraz responsds a quick point but misfires in a 10-shot rally to go down a minibreak. Shelton to serve at 2-1 with the next two points on his racket.

Alcaraz does his part and this historic quarter-final will be decided by a fifth-set tiebreaker. First man to 10 points will face Frances Tiafoe in a US Open semi-final on Friday.

Fifth set: Shelton 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 6-5 Alcaraz* (*denotes next server)

Shelton races to 30-love and “Let’s go, Ben!” chants ring through the lower bowl. Shelton gets it to 40-love, igniting the chants again (and louder), before spraying a backhand past the baseline. But the American is able to hold from there, leaving it to Alcaraz to force a deciding first-to-10-points tiebreaker.

Fifth set: *Shelton 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 5-5 Alcaraz (*denotes next server)

Alcaraz holds at love for 5-all, a game that includes a punishing 19-shot exchange that sees Shelton finally blink first. It’s 3.11am. What is life.

Fifth set: Shelton 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 5-4 Alcaraz* (*denotes next server)

An emphatic servicde game for Shelton, who holds at love in barely a minute as the match spills into its fifth hour. Alcaraz will serve to stay in the tournament after the change of ends.

Fifth set: *Shelton 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 4-4 Alcaraz (*denotes next server)

A couple of unforced errors have surfaced in Alcaraz’s game at the worst time as he goes down 15-30 on his serve. The crowd swells. And now Shelton has just painted the line with a scorching cross-court backhand winner for 15-40 and two break-point chances! This could be the match! He squanders the first after coming to net early in the rally and hitting a backhand long. And Alcaraz saves the second with another brilliant display, coming from nowhere to hit a forehand volley winner than Shelton can’t return into the court. Deuce, and could that be Shelton’s best chance at closing it out wasted?

Not so fast. Alcaraz has just double-faulted and Shelton will have a third break chance. But he can’t convert that one either, sending a running backhand into the net. Now Shelton sends a forehand long and Alcaraz is one point from the crucial hold. (They’re all crucial now.) And he wins it with a 122mph serve out wide that Shelton can’t handle. We’re on serve in the fifth!

Fifth set: Shelton 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 4-3 Alcaraz* (*denotes next server)

Shelton in trouble here. He’s quickly gone down love-30 on his serve and Alcaraz tastes blood. But the American wins two fighting points for 30-all. Shelton then hits an unreturnable serve for game point, but follows with an unforced error off the forehand for deuce. From there Shelton nails down the hold, capping it with a 144mph ace to stay on serve in the decider.

Fifth set: *Shelton 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 3-3 Alcaraz (*denotes next server)

Alcaraz closes out a drama-free hold with a 113mph ace down the middle.

And at the stroke of 2.51am it became official: this match will be the latest finish in the history of the US Open. As mentioned earlier, the previous record was 2.50am, set by Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner in their 2022 quarter-final . Alcaraz won 6-3, 6-7 (7), 6-7 (0), 7-5, 6-3 after 5hr 15min.

Fifth set: Shelton 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 3-2 Alcaraz* (*denotes next server)

With Shelton serving at 15-all, chants of “Let’s go Carlos, let’s go!” sound through the crowd. Shelton then hits a forehand volley winner, igniting his side of the crowd, but Alcaraz answeres with a backhand tracers off the ground for 30-all. articles.content:
As the official 10th day of play in New York moved deeper into the remote hours of the new morning, every passing game imbued Carlos Alcaraz with greater despair. From his focused start, Alcaraz’s intensity had flatlined and he could barely put a ball in court. He lost nine consecutive games against Ben Shelton and seemed to have nothing left.

Instead, the defending champion improbably dragged himself back into a contest that soon developed into one of the most remarkable matches of the year. The latest attempt by Alcaraz, the second seed, at orchestrating a monumental comeback was denied by a brave, defiant Shelton, the eighth seed, who refused to be shaken by his legendary rival or the looming prospect of securing the greatest win of career.

After 4hr 29min and at 3.33am, with the sun not long from rising over Flushing Meadows yet a half-full Arthur Ashe Stadium still hollering in unison until the end, Shelton ended Alcaraz’s reign with a 6-7(5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (7) victory to clinch the biggest win of his career and reach the semi-finals of the US Open.

In the aftermath of his dominant fourth-round victory against Tommy Paul, the expectations surrounding Alcaraz had risen exponentially as the seven-time grand slam title winner attempted to defend his crown. His level in the first three sets of the match, however, more faithfully reflected the fact that this was his first tournament back from a four-and-a-half-month layoff.

This was a massive opportunity for Shelton and, under such unique circumstances, he showed that he has the inner belief and resilience to rise to these occasions. He managed this match spectacularly, pairing his typically devastating serving, variation and athleticism with solid returning and steadfast consistency across five sets.

Most important, he held his nerve until the end, even after squandering essential opportunities deep in the final set. “Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old,” he said. “It’s always fun being on the court against him. It’s ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes. The most enjoyable match that I’ve had in my career, for sure.”

Alcaraz left everything on the court, his lack of physical preparation also reflected in periods of fatigue and even vomiting into his towel on the court towards the end of the fourth set. Afterwards, he refused to leave the tournament downbeat after being part of such an immense battle against one of the best players in the world so early in his comeback from a serious injury. “As I said before the tournament began, my expectation was to go there, compete, play in these kind of matches for me being healthy,” he said.

“It was close. It was close. So I’m just not going to be disappointed about don’t getting the win at the end. You know, I’m just happy. I’m just proud about myself, about how I fought. After the third set, physically I was really tired, but you know I found a way to push myself up and physically giving extra.”

As a result of Alcaraz’s defeat, a new US Open champion will be crowned: 23 years after Andy Roddick’s triumph here, the last time an American man tasted victory at any grand slam tournament, Shelton will face his compatriot and friend Frances Tiafoe in a wide-open draw. “I was playing against one of the best – he is a beast,” Alcaraz said. “Shelton is an unbelievable player, powerful. He just managed how to play really, really well in every situation, so credit to him. I leave the court happy. I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed.”

There are times when the tennis authorities make self-sabotaging decisions regarding scheduling, but sometimes it is just impossible to contain or plan for the greatness of this sport. This is, without doubt, one of the most incredible days of tennis in years. All four quarter-finals on Tuesday extended to deciding sets with Aryna Sabalenka, Tiafoe and Jessica Pegula each dragging themselves through spectacular comeback victories against Linda Noskova, Alex Michelsen and Emma Navarro respectively.

Alcaraz and Shelton did not start until 11.04pm, but over their subsequent four and a half hours on the court that was soundtracked by a delirious, raucous crowd until the very end, their battle provided the perfect climax to 16 hours of greatness, a night and morning that the thousands of roaring fans still present until the bitter end will never forget.

“It was just enjoyable to be a part of that match,” Shelton said. “Obviously the level of tennis, how long the match was going, the fight that it was, how even of a match it was back and forth throughout, I think that that’s something that we can appreciate. Win or lose, we would have a smile on our face.”

Instead, the defending champion improbably dragged himself back into a contest that soon developed into one of the most remarkable matches of the year. The latest attempt by Alcaraz, the second seed, at orchestrating a monumental comeback was denied by a brave, defiant Shelton, the eighth seed, who refused to be shaken by his legendary rival or the looming prospect of securing the greatest win of career.

After 4hr 29min and at 3.33am, with the sun not long from rising over Flushing Meadows yet a half-full Arthur Ashe Stadium still hollering in unison until the end, Shelton ended Alcaraz’s reign with a 6-7(5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (7) victory to clinch the biggest win of his career and reach the semi-finals of the US Open.

In the aftermath of his dominant fourth-round victory against Tommy Paul, the expectations surrounding Alcaraz had risen exponentially as the seven-time grand slam title winner attempted to defend his crown. His level in the first three sets of the match, however, more faithfully reflected the fact that this was his first tournament back from a four-and-a-half-month layoff.

This was a massive opportunity for Shelton and, under such unique circumstances, he showed that he has the inner belief and resilience to rise to these occasions. He managed this match spectacularly, pairing his typically devastating serving, variation and athleticism with solid returning and steadfast consistency across five sets.

Most important, he held his nerve until the end, even after squandering essential opportunities deep in the final set. “Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old,” he said. “It’s always fun being on the court against him. It’s ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes. The most enjoyable match that I’ve had in my career, for sure.”

Alcaraz left everything on the court, his lack of physical preparation also reflected in periods of fatigue and even vomiting into his towel on the court towards the end of the fourth set. Afterwards, he refused to leave the tournament downbeat after being part of such an immense battle against one of the best players in the world so early in his comeback from a serious injury. “As I said before the tournament began, my expectation was to go there, compete, play in these kind of matches for me being healthy,” he said.

“It was close. It was close. So I’m just not going to be disappointed about don’t getting the win at the end. You know, I’m just happy. I’m just proud about myself, about how I fought. After the third set, physically I was really tired, but you know I found a way to push myself up and physically giving extra.”

As a result of Alcaraz’s defeat, a new US Open champion will be crowned: 23 years after Andy Roddick’s triumph here, the last time an American man tasted victory at any grand slam tournament, Shelton will face his compatriot and friend Frances Tiafoe in a wide-open draw. “I was playing against one of the best – he is a beast,” Alcaraz said. “Shelton is an unbelievable player, powerful. He just managed how to play really, really well in every situation, so credit to him. I leave the court happy. I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed.”

There are times when the tennis authorities make self-sabotaging decisions regarding scheduling, but sometimes it is just impossible to contain or plan for the greatness of this sport. This is, without doubt, one of the most incredible days of tennis in years. All four quarter-finals on Tuesday extended to deciding sets with Aryna Sabalenka, Tiafoe and Jessica Pegula each dragging themselves through spectacular comeback victories against Linda Noskova, Alex Michelsen and Emma Navarro respectively.

Alcaraz and Shelton did not start until 11.04pm, but over their subsequent four and a half hours on the court that was soundtracked by a delirious, raucous crowd until the very end, their battle provided the perfect climax to 16 hours of greatness, a night and morning that the thousands of roaring fans still present until the bitter end will never forget.

“It was just enjoyable to be a part of that match,” Shelton said. “Obviously the level of tennis, how long the match was going, the fight that it was, how even of a match it was back and forth throughout, I think that that’s something that we can appreciate. Win or lose, we would have a smile on our face.”

articles.content:
The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happen

Quarterbacks living under center. The NFL has developed into a shotgun league, where most quarterbacks take the majority of their snaps three to seven yards away from the center. But the increase in efficiency when it comes to snaps taken right behind the center should have coaches directing their quarterbacks to do more of it. Matthew Stafford, Caleb Williams, and Sam Darnold led the way in 2025, and others will follow. DF

Superteams. The Rams have pushed their chips to the middle of the table by loading up on high-end veterans and deferring much of the cost to future years. Myles Garrett and the unretired Aaron Donald join Stafford, Puka Nacua and a secondary reinforced by Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. Superteams are never a sure thing in the NFL, but the Rams’ terrifyingly stacked roster looks awfully close. BAG

Super Bowl sequel hype , the year the scriptwriters lay a path for a Rams-Bengals rematch in Los Angeles. Both teams have gone to considerable lengths to shore up the defensive side of the ball, with the Rams swinging a mega trade for Garrett on the heels of the Bengals’ draft-week swap for Pro Bowl tackle Dexter Lawrence. AL

Finally saying goodbye to Aaron Rodgers . Let’s forget all the weirdness around the latter years of his career and remember Rodgers as simply one of the best to ever do it. Maybe with Mike McCarthy calling plays again, he can keep Pittsburgh in contention for a wildcard. Even if he fails, you can guarantee seeing some of the old magic in his final season in the NFL. GS

This is the second straight season I’ve pushed the Vikings here, and for the same reasons – the NFC North is the league’s most competitive division, and there is no outstanding candidate at quarterback. Brian Flores’s defense will be marvelous as it always is, and were it not for his ongoing lawsuit against the league , he’d probably be a head coach right now. A three-man quarterback competition is not the best way to maximize one’s competitive window, though. DF

Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb are back for an offense that can put up points with almost anybody. But the NFC is deep and unforgiving and the Cowboys ’ front seven looks alarmingly short of difference-makers beyond star defensive tackle Quinnen Williams and Rashan Gary. Nine wins, constant frustration and a third straight January on the couch sounds about right. BAG

The Vikings ’ defense always gives them a chance, and their offensive skill players are elite. It just comes down to what Murray can give them and, historically, that’s been a lot of inconsistency. AL

It will be a battle for Ben Johnson to keep the lightning in the bottle with a Bears defense that thrived on takeaways rather than fundamentals last season. They haven’t made many significant moves – outside first-round safety Dillon Thieneman – to tune things up, then the impressive offense could be let down with a near miss in the wildcard race. GS

It’s easy to forget that in the 2021 season, the Bengals lost the Super Bowl by three points, and in 2022, they lost the AFC Championship game by the same margin. Those close calls were followed by matching 9-8 seasons in 2023 and 2024, and last season’s 6-11 faceplant. But if Joe Burrow can stay healthy, these Bengals have a ton of talent on both sides of the ball (led by new defensive line monster Lawrence). DF

Justin Herbert is class and Mike McDaniel’s arrival as offensive coordinator will add some imagination and flair to the offense. But winning 11 games still leaves you overshadowed when Denver’s complete roster and Patrick Mahomes’ Kansas City headline your division. The Chargers are quiet contenders hiding in plain sight. BAG

Last I checked, the Chiefs not only return Patrick Mahomes – the QB standard before the ACL injury (hardly the career killers they used to be) – but also Eric Bieniemy, the offensive coordinator who held players accountable and infused the team’s gameplay with so much confidence and whimsy. AL

Baker Mayfield was quietly brilliant last season and the Buccaneers have a strong roster across the board that finished 8-9 after a 6-2 start because of a number of key players missing time through injury. A bit of luck with the injury bug and the Bucs could spring a surprise. GS

The Browns’ quarterback situation. What else could it be? At this point, the Browns may as well bring Manziel back to add even more of a tragic comic cast to the whole thing. Head coach Todd Monken naming Deshaun Watson the Week 1 starter after Watson played horribly and alienated the fanbase in the preseason – never mind the horrid off-field history for which Watson has never taken an ounce of accountability – is merely the first level of Dante’s Inferno. DF

Cleveland naming Watson their Week 1 starter . A $230m albatross coming off multiple achilles tears would have been a risky first choice even if he’d been playing well before getting hurt. The Browns’ decision to roster three other quarterbacks, including Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve, feels prescient here. BAG

Anthony Richardson survived trade rumors and played well enough in camp to win the Colts’ backup QB job. But I say the detente only holds up as long as Daniel Jones’s health, which has never been the greatest, and Richardson’s uneven play in relief makes him a lame duck QB all over again – and his controversial behavior gives the organization cover for the bad fit once more. AL

The Browns missing Garrett’s tremendous pass rush and leadership is a recipe for a very tricky season if they make a slow start. And with Watson starting at quarterback they most likely will. GS

Drake Maye, QB, New England Patriots. While I don’t have the Patriots winning the AFC East this season, I think that with the additions of receivers AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs, and coming off a full season in Josh McDaniels’ offense, Maye has everything he needs to take the next step to become an unquestioned Top 10 quarterback. He was exactly that until the Patriots faced a murderers’ row of defenses in the playoffs and his protection fell apart, but the growth he showed in everything from reading the field to taking disguised coverages apart presaged that next level. DF

Lamar Jackson, QB, Baltimore Ravens. The Ravens enter a new era under first-year coach Jesse Minter, but their fortunes still revolve around the NFL’s most disruptive player. The 29-year-old Jackson can unhinge defenses with his arm, legs or simply the threat of either. If Baltimore can get to 12 or 13 wins, he becomes the best bet to enter the exclusive club of three-time MVPs. BAG

Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. Now that he has a defense behind him again, Joe Cool can get back to lighting up the scoreboard and his cigar after the dubs. AL

Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. The quarterback finished last year showing some of his best work, so this could be Burrow’s time with incredible weapons Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins at his disposal. GS

Caleb Downs, DB, Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys’ 2025 defense was one of the worst in recent memory, which is why they replaced Matt Eberflus with Christian Parker as defensive coordinator. Parker’s background with the Philadelphia Eagles and defensive wizard Vic Fangio should pay immediate dividends, and Downs, the Ohio State alum selected with the 11th overall pick, should thrive in Parker’s concepts. DF

Jadarian Price, RB, Seattle Seahawks. With Kenneth Walker III gone and Zach Charbonnet starting the season on the Physically Unable to Perform list, the Seahawks will plug-and-play their first-round draft pick from Notre Dame into a backfield fresh off a Super Bowl title. BAG

Jeremiyah Love, RB, Arizona Cardinals. The Notre Dame prospect shouldn’t lack for opportunities to get the ball off tackle, in space or however else coach Mike LaFleur seeks to make use of the Saquon Barkley clone he simply couldn’t pass up in this year’s draft. AL

Carnell Tate, WR, Tennessee Titans . The No 4 pick has the total package of speed, route running and size. Tate caught the eye in training camp working with second-year quarterback Cam Ward. He will continue to do so throughout 2026. GS

I’m picking the Bills for one reason, and it’s not Josh Allen – it’s Jim Leonhard. Buffalo’s new defensive coordinator is one of the finest minds in football, and he’ll have that defense asserting itself in ways it never did under Sean McDermott. New England will still be up there after 2025’s Cinderella season, but a tougher schedule and possible regression when it comes to their unusual injury luck should have them taking a step back. DF

New England won it last year and added star wideout Brown, but a regression from 14 wins is almost inevitable even if the Super Bowl loser’s curse has mostly been debunked . The Bills have Allen, DJ Moore and enough defensive talent for first-year coach Joe Brady to take back a division the Bills owned for five straight years before last season. BAG

Not because the Bills are necessarily better than the team that beat them to the top last year. But because New England’s schedule is so much tougher this year, and one loss makes all the difference in this chilly rivalry. AL

A straight shootout between New England and Buffalo. With fresh ideas from Brady, the Bills could have an important edge but there’s not much wriggle room in their opening five games against the Texans, Lions, Chargers, Patriots and Rams. Escaping with a winning record from that run would provide a solid platform to regain dominance. GS

Trading for Lawrence was the splashy story of the Bengals ’ offseason, but there’s a lot more to like here – especially if Burrow can stay healthy. If he can, I like the Bengals to outpace the Ravens and Steelers based on star power with receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, and a defense that has a lot of ascending players. DF

Minter has been dealt an enviable hand with Jackson, Derrick Henry and a roster built to win now. Cincinnati should push them, but the Ravens ’ combination of quarterback play, running game and defensive stability remains the division’s safest bet. BAG

The Bengals . Here’s a sentence no one’s ever written until now: Mike Brown, the NFL’s resident cheapskate, is all in. AL

If Burrow just has a full season working behind an improved offensive line, then the Bengals have a great shot at unseating the Ravens. Their schedule is soft enough that they should be aiming for well over 10 wins. GS

I’m taking the Texans over the Jaguars because of a defense that needs no schematic tricks to upend enemy offenses – they’re good enough to just line up and go right at you. All the Texans need from quarterback CJ Stroud is a level of play a bit above league-average. DF

The Texans defense is one of the NFL’s best with Will Anderson Jr, Derek Stingley Jr and Kamari Lassiter leading the way. Whether Stroud and the offense can hold up their end of the bargain remains the rub, but it should be enough in this middling division. BAG

The Jaguars repeatedly found ways to win tight games in 2025, giving a young team meaningful late-game experience – and a plausible foundation to turn last year’s surge into a deep postseason run. AL

The defense returns almost unchanged after a brilliant 2025 with some good additions in safety Reed Blankenship and rookie run-stopper Kayden McDonald. The Texans have quality and consistency a level above the messy Jaguars and Colts. GS

I really like what new Chargers offensive coordinator McDaniel will do for Herbert, and I expect the Chiefs to rebound to a point from last season’s disaster. But the 2025 Broncos got all the way to the AFC Championship game, and they may have progressed further had quarterback Bo Nix not suffered a broken ankle in the divisional round. Now, Nix has a new best buddy to help him – former Miami Dolphins receiver Jaylen Waddle, who gives that offense a level of vertical juice it hasn’t had before. DF

They’d probably be defending NFL champions if not for Nix’s untimely injury in the playoffs. The Broncos defense remains elite, the offensive line is right there with it and the addition of Waddle gives them another weapon on offense alongside Courtland Sutton. Nix’s mission with the AFC’s deepest roster boils down to three words: do no harm. BAG

The Chargers made many of the right moves this offseason: keeping most of their receiving corps intact, adding David Njoku and big-play tailback Keaton Mitchell, and rebuilding the interior offensive line. Losing new center Tyler Biadasz to injury is a major blow, but if the line holds together well enough, Herbert and a deep, balanced roster give the Bolts a real chance to edge Kansas City and Denver. AL

The Chiefs and Chargers should be well in the mix but the Broncos still have the edge after last year’s dominance before Nix went down in the playoffs. GS

The Cowboys bag the crown based on an offense that’s already fully loaded, and a defense that should be worlds better than in 2025. They are the Inverse Houston Texans in that all that defense has to do is play at a pretty good level to blow a lot of opponents away. DF

Brown is gone and Jalen Hurts will be working with his seventh different play-caller in as many NFL seasons, but the Eagles ’ institutional strength has been the envy of the NFC East for decades now. A potentially top-five defense and a rejuvenated ground game featuring Saquon Barkley will provide enough margin for error to outlast a division filled with flawed rivals. BAG

With Brown and coordinator Kevin Patullo gone, the Eagles offense should fly again behind Barkley and Hurts – in make or break year mode not that long after leading the team to Super Bowl glory. AL

The Cowboys are hardly a sleeping giant, but if the defense is as reborn as defensive tackle Williams claims it is then maybe Dallas can finally balance the books with their dynamic offense and reclaim the division. GS

Close your eyes and throw a dart at the NFL’s toughest division, and you have a 25% chance of being right. The Lions, Packers, and Vikings all have reason for hope, but if Bears head coach Ben Johnson can refine quarterback Caleb Williams, and Dennis Allen’s defense can improve over last season’s boom-or-bust results – they led the NFL in turnover differential , but ranked 23rd in points allowed – it’s Chicago’s time to shine. DF

Chicago may be the trendy pick and Green Bay dangerous floaters, but the Lions still have enough offensive firepower and strength along the line of scrimmage to hold them off in the NFL’s deepest division. BAG

The Lions were burned by injuries last year and still stayed in the playoff hunt almost to the end. They are positioned for a rebound, with more of their core available and one of the league’s easiest schedules – a chance to bank early wins while key pieces work their way back from early-season absences. AL

The Packers remain without Micah Parsons until at least Week 5 but a look at their first four opponents – the Vikings, Jets, Falcons and Buccaneers – points to a hot start. GS

Mayfield was outstanding in the first half of the 2025 season before his own injuries, and the injuries of those around him, took their toll. The Buccaneers started the season 6-2 before falling off to 8-9. With better luck things should look quite a bit better in 2026. DF

The Buccaneers have the most settled quarterback situation, enough skill-position talent and a defense that’s just good enough. Carolina are the likeliest threat while neither Atlanta nor rebuilding New Orleans have enough to mount a serious challenge. BAG

There’s little incentive to go against the Buccaneers , the gold standard in the league’s most volatile division. AL

Off the back of late-season success in 2025, the Saints will be feeling good about their chances. If second-year quarterback Tyler Shough maintains his upward trajectory they should be confident. GS

While there are reasons to question the ultimate validity of the Rams ’ “all-in” approach that culminated with the return of Donald, there’s enough in the hypothetical to give Sean McVay’s team a slight edge over the Seahawks – if only because Seattle didn’t follow their Super Bowl win by radically stocking their defense as the Rams did. DF

There are legitimate durability questions around the aging Stafford and the returning Donald for the Rams . But it’s hard to imagine anyone challenging a roster tricked out with as much high-end talent as any NFL team in years. Anything short of a division title would qualify as a serious underachievement. BAG

The Rams . With apologies to the reigning Super Bowl champs, the moves GM Les Snead and Co made in the offseason to shore up their defense are eerily similar to the big swings they took in the 2021 season. And we all know how that turned out. AL

Donald and Garrett have five defensive player of the year awards between them and link up with former Super Bowl winners from the Chiefs in Watson and McDuffie. The Rams are stacked and then some. GS

Rams over Bills. The Rams’ “ F Them Picks ” philosophy served them well when they gave up a ton of draft capital for Stafford, Jalen Ramsey, and Von Miller, and they won the Super Bowl as a result. If the 2026 Rams find that their go-for-broke philosophy works once again with a radical reshuffling of their defense, it’s hard to bet against them, because the offense was already so on point. DF

Rams over Broncos. The Rams have spent the offseason putting together a star-studded roster unlike anything we’ve seen in years, adding Garrett, McDuffie and Watson before Donald decided he wasn’t finished after all. Denver’s elite defense is capable of making it ugly, but Sean McVay’s embarrassment of riches on both sides of the ball will ultimately prove too much. BAG

Bengals over Rams. Burrow avenges the biggest loss in his career, and it’s in no small part thanks to Brown and player personnel director Duke Tobin pulling the trigger one last time on a piece that helps neutralize the effects of the Garrett-Donald pocket collapse (an extra guard, a fullback – don’t hold me to specifics). The confusion over what to make of Zac Taylor as a Super Bowl-winning coach quickly gives way to the confusion over what to make of a championship parade festooned with tributes to the world’s weirdest chili . In other words, the renovations on ancient Paycor Stadium pay for themselves . AL

Broncos over Rams. Denver can argue they were a broken ankle away from the Super Bowl last season. Handily for the Broncos they come back with almost an identical roster this year. They kept starting running back JK Dobbins and brought in Waddle to help out Sutton. The Broncos already have the AFC’s best defense to go with a sublime offensive line and exciting weapons that can take down the Rams. GS
