Trading for Lawrence was the splashy story of the Bengals ’ offseason, but there’s a lot more to like here – especially if Burrow can stay healthy. If he can, I like the Bengals to outpace the Ravens and Steelers based on star power with receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, and a defense that has a lot of ascending players. DF

Minter has been dealt an enviable hand with Jackson, Derrick Henry and a roster built to win now. Cincinnati should push them, but the Ravens ’ combination of quarterback play, running game and defensive stability remains the division’s safest bet. BAG
The Bengals . Here’s a sentence no one’s ever written until now: Mike Brown, the NFL’s resident cheapskate, is all in. AL

If Burrow just has a full season working behind an improved offensive line, then the Bengals have a great shot at unseating the Ravens. Their schedule is soft enough that they should be aiming for well over 10 wins. GS

I’m taking the Texans over the Jaguars because of a defense that needs no schematic tricks to upend enemy offenses – they’re good enough to just line up and go right at you. All the Texans need from quarterback CJ Stroud is a level of play a bit above league-average. DF

The Texans defense is one of the NFL’s best with Will Anderson Jr, Derek Stingley Jr and Kamari Lassiter leading the way. Whether Stroud and the offense can hold up their end of the bargain remains the rub, but it should be enough in this middling division. BAG
The Jaguars repeatedly found ways to win tight games in 2025, giving a young team meaningful late-game experience – and a plausible foundation to turn last year’s surge into a deep postseason run. AL

The defense returns almost unchanged after a brilliant 2025 with some good additions in safety Reed Blankenship and rookie run-stopper Kayden McDonald. The Texans have quality and consistency a level above the messy Jaguars and Colts. GS

I really like what new Chargers offensive coordinator McDaniel will do for Herbert, and I expect the Chiefs to rebound to a point from last season’s disaster. But the 2025 Broncos got all the way to the AFC Championship game, and they may have progressed further had quarterback Bo Nix not suffered a broken ankle in the divisional round. Now, Nix has a new best buddy to help him – former Miami Dolphins receiver Jaylen Waddle, who gives that offense a level of vertical juice it hasn’t had before. DF

They’d probably be defending NFL champions if not for Nix’s untimely injury in the playoffs. The Broncos defense remains elite, the offensive line is right there with it and the addition of Waddle gives them another weapon on offense alongside Courtland Sutton. Nix’s mission with the AFC’s deepest roster boils down to three words: do no harm. BAG

The Chargers made many of the right moves this offseason: keeping most of their receiving corps intact, adding David Njoku and big-play tailback Keaton Mitchell, and rebuilding the interior offensive line. Losing new center Tyler Biadasz to injury is a major blow, but if the line holds together well enough, Herbert and a deep, balanced roster give the Bolts a real chance to edge Kansas City and Denver. AL
The Chiefs and Chargers should be well in the mix but the Broncos still have the edge after last year’s dominance before Nix went down in the playoffs. GS

The Cowboys bag the crown based on an offense that’s already fully loaded, and a defense that should be worlds better than in 2025. They are the Inverse Houston Texans in that all that defense has to do is play at a pretty good level to blow a lot of opponents away. DF

Brown is gone and Jalen Hurts will be working with his seventh different play-caller in as many NFL seasons, but the Eagles ’ institutional strength has been the envy of the NFC East for decades now. A potentially top-five defense and a rejuvenated ground game featuring Saquon Barkley will provide enough margin for error to outlast a division filled with flawed rivals. BAG
With Brown and coordinator Kevin Patullo gone, the Eagles offense should fly again behind Barkley and Hurts – in make or break year mode not that long after leading the team to Super Bowl glory. AL

The Cowboys are hardly a sleeping giant, but if the defense is as reborn as defensive tackle Williams claims it is then maybe Dallas can finally balance the books with their dynamic offense and reclaim the division. GS

Close your eyes and throw a dart at the NFL’s toughest division, and you have a 25% chance of being right. The Lions, Packers, and Vikings all have reason for hope, but if Bears head coach Ben Johnson can refine quarterback Caleb Williams, and Dennis Allen’s defense can improve over last season’s boom-or-bust results – they led the NFL in turnover differential , but ranked 23rd in points allowed – it’s Chicago’s time to shine. DF

Chicago may be the trendy pick and Green Bay dangerous floaters, but the Lions still have enough offensive firepower and strength along the line of scrimmage to hold them off in the NFL’s deepest division. BAG

The Lions were burned by injuries last year and still stayed in the playoff hunt almost to the end. They are positioned for a rebound, with more of their core available and one of the league’s easiest schedules – a chance to bank early wins while key pieces work their way back from early-season absences. AL
The Packers remain without Micah Parsons until at least Week 5 but a look at their first four opponents – the Vikings, Jets, Falcons and Buccaneers – points to a hot start. GS

Mayfield was outstanding in the first half of the 2025 season before his own injuries, and the injuries of those around him, took their toll. The Buccaneers started the season 6-2 before falling off to 8-9. With better luck things should look quite a bit better in 2026. DF

The Buccaneers have the most settled quarterback situation, enough skill-position talent and a defense that’s just good enough. Carolina are the likeliest threat while neither Atlanta nor rebuilding New Orleans have enough to mount a serious challenge. BAG
There’s little incentive to go against the Buccaneers , the gold standard in the league’s most volatile division. AL
Off the back of late-season success in 2025, the Saints will be feeling good about their chances. If second-year quarterback Tyler Shough maintains his upward trajectory they should be confident. GS

While there are reasons to question the ultimate validity of the Rams ’ “all-in” approach that culminated with the return of Donald, there’s enough in the hypothetical to give Sean McVay’s team a slight edge over the Seahawks – if only because Seattle didn’t follow their Super Bowl win by radically stocking their defense as the Rams did. DF

There are legitimate durability questions around the aging Stafford and the returning Donald for the Rams . But it’s hard to imagine anyone challenging a roster tricked out with as much high-end talent as any NFL team in years. Anything short of a division title would qualify as a serious underachievement. BAG

The Rams . With apologies to the reigning Super Bowl champs, the moves GM Les Snead and Co made in the offseason to shore up their defense are eerily similar to the big swings they took in the 2021 season. And we all know how that turned out. AL
Donald and Garrett have five defensive player of the year awards between them and link up with former Super Bowl winners from the Chiefs in Watson and McDuffie. The Rams are stacked and then some. GS

Rams over Bills. The Rams’ “ F Them Picks ” philosophy served them well when they gave up a ton of draft capital for Stafford, Jalen Ramsey, and Von Miller, and they won the Super Bowl as a result. If the 2026 Rams find that their go-for-broke philosophy works once again with a radical reshuffling of their defense, it’s hard to bet against them, because the offense was already so on point. DF

Rams over Broncos. The Rams have spent the offseason putting together a star-studded roster unlike anything we’ve seen in years, adding Garrett, McDuffie and Watson before Donald decided he wasn’t finished after all. Denver’s elite defense is capable of making it ugly, but Sean McVay’s embarrassment of riches on both sides of the ball will ultimately prove too much. BAG

Bengals over Rams. Burrow avenges the biggest loss in his career, and it’s in no small part thanks to Brown and player personnel director Duke Tobin pulling the trigger one last time on a piece that helps neutralize the effects of the Garrett-Donald pocket collapse (an extra guard, a fullback – don’t hold me to specifics). The confusion over what to make of Zac Taylor as a Super Bowl-winning coach quickly gives way to the confusion over what to make of a championship parade festooned with tributes to the world’s weirdest chili . In other words, the renovations on ancient Paycor Stadium pay for themselves . AL

Broncos over Rams. Denver can argue they were a broken ankle away from the Super Bowl last season. Handily for the Broncos they come back with almost an identical roster this year. They kept starting running back JK Dobbins and brought in Waddle to help out Sutton. The Broncos already have the AFC’s best defense to go with a sublime offensive line and exciting weapons that can take down the Rams. GS

articles.content:
A remote 18th-century chapel deep in Sami lands is the goal of the Präststigen, a 37-mile trail that traverses some of the country’s most spectacular scenery

I wasn’t exactly in “Sunday best”, but I had made some effort. Well, I’d changed my underwear for the first time in a couple of days and given myself a baby-wipe bath. Still, as we filed into the chapel at Alkavare, I felt more a member of an expedition than a congregation. We sat on the low wooden benches, waterproof jackets rustling and leather walking boots stamping on the flagstone floor to keep warm. Fortunately, the priest, Mogens Amstrup Jacobsen, appeared to be a “man of the Gore-Tex”, as well as a man of the cloth, as he unzipped his own black rain jacket to reveal his dog collar. As the service began, the Arctic wind whipped through cracks in the dry stone walls, insulated only with reindeer hair, and candles flickered in their brass sconces.

I had hiked to Alkavare following the Präststigen , or “Priests’ trail”, a 37-mile (60km) route from Kvikkjokk that could stake a claim as Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route, and certainly one of its most beautiful. The Präststigen follows the path that priests would once have taken to the chapel, built in 1788, to perform a service each summer, and today, on the last weekend in July, intrepid hikers and perseverant pilgrims can attend that same service.

Alkavare sits on the western border of Sweden’s Sarek national park, home to many of the country’s highest mountains and steepest valleys, yet with no campsites or tourist huts and only scant sections of the more famous Kungsleden trail. There are no other marked paths and to hike here means wild camping, a heavy backpack and a sense of adventure. It was described by famed Swedish diplomat Dag Hammarskjöld in 1926 as vår sista stora vildmark – “ our last great wilderness”.

“I hate it when people use the term ‘wilderness’,” Christian Heimrot from Laponia Adventures, a local guiding operator, told me, as I joined him on the research exhibition for a new Präststigen group trip launching next year. “This is a living landscape, people have lived, worked and shaped this land for thousands of years.” Indeed, Sarek national park , (as part of the wider Laponia region), was recognised as a Unsesco World Heritage Site in 1996 for both its cultural and natural value.

The Sami, Europe’s last Indigenous population, have braided themselves into these landscapes as tightly and beautifully as the thread of pewter in their traditional handicrafts. The Sami word for the Laponia area is Sápmi , the same word they use to refer to themselves, highlighting the indelible link between people and their environment. Sarek sits on the Sami’s traditional reindeer herding grounds. While they might now use motorcycles and snowmobiles to follow and herd the reindeer, their knowledge of and kinship with this landscape remains undimmed.

So, not wilderness, then, but certainly wild. To even reach the start of the Präststigen, I had crossed the Arctic Circle on the road north from Luleå, met with Christian at his warehouse in Jokkmokk (home to the famous Sami winter markets each February) to load up our rucksacks for the six-night trip, and journeyed an hour farther west to the town of Kvikkjokk. From there the trailhead was a short boat ride across Sakkat lake.

The first section of the trail climbed steeply, switchbacks tightly coiled in birch woodland; wild blueberries and cloudberries littered the path. Eventually we left the woodland and reached the ridge for our first proper view of Sarek. Away to the north was the cloud-covered summit of Bårddetjåhkkå, where in 1911 Swedish geologist Axel Hamberg built an observatory to conduct meteorological and glacial studies.

We slept soundly, as we eased into the rhythms of wild camping – water collected from a gin-clear lake, a hearty supper of reindeer stew, and an eye mask to keep out the midnight sun. The next day we hiked deeper into Sarek via the Vállevágge, the skies the blue of the Swedish flag, the silence only disrupted by the occasional breath of wind.

We were following the guidebook Priest’s Path by Hans Fowelin (currently only published in Swedish), and while there was no marked trail, Fowelin had plotted a path of cairns we were supposedly to follow. While some were solidly built square towers, most were little more than one rock propped up against another, mere whispers of waymarkers in a landscape of scree and moraine.

Alongside the familiar buttercups and heather there were bright blue blossoms of mountain gentian, red ptarmigan berries and otherworldly looking wild angelica, a source of vitamin C for the Sami. Sarek was visited by botanist Carl Linnaeus during his epic expedition through northern Sweden in 1732, and the first part of the Priest’s trail is sometimes referred to as Linnaeus’s trail.

On our fourth day of hiking Alkavare chapel appeared on a bluff above the glacial blue waters of Alggajavvre lake, surrounded by high peaks and valleys. It was utterly beautiful. I had a grin on my wind-burnt face for most of the day, one that even wading across rivers (a common feature of hiking in Sarek), shin-high in glacial meltwater, failed to dim.

After rowing across the Miellätno river, using one of the rowing boats left on each bank by the park rangers, we climbed up to the chapel late on Saturday evening where Jacobsen greeted us with a beaming smile.

Over tea, he told us he had been dropped off by helicopter at Alkavare with his family on Friday morning and this was his first time leading the service here. Others in the diocese no longer volunteered. “It is physical, hard work and the days are long,” he said, before heading off to re-tar the chapel’s roof and fix one of the rowing boats that had come loose and floated away down the river – returned, later, swinging beneath a helicopter.

Sunday mass began promptly at 11am the following morning for our small band of pilgrims (we numbered 11 in total, including the priest). The altar had a simple wooden cross and cloths on loan from the church in Jokkmokk. They were in the poster paint palate of traditional Sami clothing and a reminder that it was for the Sami that the chapel had been originally built – not an act of benevolence, but as part of the forced Christianisation and eradication of their shamanistic beliefs in the 18th century.

After the service we sat outside for coffee and pastries, before beginning our hike home. Christian was keen that we hiked via Sweden’s point of inaccessibility or otillgänglighetspunkten , just over the border from Sarek in the Padjelanta national park. This is the country’s point furthest from any road or town, about 31 miles (50km) in fact, and is often cited as western Europe’s remotest too. Marked with no cairn or monument, just a circle of quartz stones and a trio of reindeer antlers, it felt no more or less remote than most of the previous week’s hiking. And I was struck that what made Sarek and the Präststigen special wasn’t just the scenery, as beautiful as it was, it was the people – the Sami, Hamberg and Linneaus, and the motley congregation we’d briefly joined, and it was a route firmly deserving of more visitors. “I told you,” Christian said, grinning, “It isn’t a wilderness.”

The trip was provided by Laponia Adventures , wh ich will lead a guided, small-group trip along the Priest’s Path to Alkavare in July 2027, and offers equipment rental and advice for independent hikers. For more information on Sarek national park and northern Sweden, visit arcticsweden.com

articles.title: A moment that changed me: I spent a day with some naturists – and it cured my shy bladder
articles.summary: For decades, I had been haunted by paruresis, an inability to urinate in public toilets. But that day of nakedness suddenly, surprisingly, led me to shed my inhibitions For as long as I can remember, I’ve suffered from a condition called paruresis – also known as shy bladder syndrome. articles.content:
For decades, I had been haunted by paruresis, an inability to urinate in public toilets. But that day of nakedness suddenly, surprisingly, led me to shed my inhibitions

F or as long as I can remember, I’ve suffered from a condition called paruresis – also known as shy bladder syndrome. This means that, unless I’m alone in public toilets, I cannot pee, however badly I need to go. I developed tactics to deal with this, such as loitering outside the gents if I see someone going in, so that I can walk in as they walk out. But if someone follows me in, I find I’m just standing there, which I worry looks odd.

I’m a writer, so am often out and about meeting people in cafes, hotels and at events. My agricultural background means I also meet a lot of my interviewees on farms – but at least there I could pop behind a hedge if I needed to go, and be assured of privacy.

It was while I was doing research for a book on the spiritual connections humans once had with the land that I stumbled across the Christian Naturist Fellowship: a network of people who believe that Christianity and naturism are entirely compatible. Here, I thought, were a community who clearly get closer to nature than most – I was keen to meet them.

One of their committee members, Nigel, suggested I visit his naturist club near Colchester. So one Saturday morning in 2025, I set off to discover what Christian naturists really think and do. He had said that I’d not have to strip off – many don’t on their first visit – but when the time came, that is exactly what I did.

I’d been naked in public once before, but then I’d been one of more than 3,000 people who, in 2016, had stripped off in a Hull city centre park at dawn, daubed themselves with blue body paint, and been photographed by Spencer Tunick as a visual celebration of the city’s relationship with the sea. Then, I’d enjoyed the anonymity of being one in a crowd and, strangely, it still felt as if I was wearing something, albeit just blue paint. Visiting a small naturists’ collective would be different.

After arriving at Springwood Sun Club, Nigel greeted me wearing a warm smile – and a pair of shorts. As it happened, he was not in a rush to shed his clothes either, and we both walked to the clubhouse fully dressed. It could have been any social club, except that the foursome playing miniten outside were in the buff.

Nigel then took me to a clearing in the woods, where he told me he believed it important to touch the ground with your bare feet – so we slipped off our shoes and socks and gave it a go. He introduced me to several of the other naturists and, after a while, I began to feel a little overdressed. I suggested that the time had come for me to go with the flow; I returned to my car and stripped off, while Nigel popped into his cabin to do the same. When I nipped to the loos later on, I thankfully found them to be empty – although walking in with no clothes on, and not having to zip up before washing my hands, did feel strange.

Before I left for home, our conversation returned to Christianity and, knowing that I was a Quaker, Nigel invited me to come back as a visiting speaker at an interfaith event Springwood was hosting later that summer. On my second visit, I felt no hesitation and stripped off on arrival.

My inhibitions about being seen without clothes left me after that first visit – but, to my surprise, so too did my paruresis. Looking back, I realise that it had always been connected to a fear of nakedness, of people being able to see me urinate. I remember how, at primary school, I would refuse to use the school toilets, despite clearly needing a wee.

I stopped at a garden centre for a coffee on my way home and, when visiting the loos, was horrified to discover that only the centre urinal of three was not being used. But rather than feel so embarrassed that I was forced to walk out, I stepped forward and, astonishingly, had no problem at all. A few days later, visiting Norwich, I discovered once more that I could pee in company. Since then, I’ve not experienced any difficulty, no matter how busy the toilets. Spending a day with the naturists seemed to have cured a problem that had haunted me for decades.

My time with the Christian Naturist Fellowship also helped me realise that people really do come in all shapes and sizes, and that very few of us have the kind of physique we are encouraged to aspire to, especially by social media. Dipping my toe into this world made me realise how, when clothes are shed, so too can we let go of inhibitions and pretences – and even lifelong anxieties.

F or as long as I can remember, I’ve suffered from a condition called paruresis – also known as shy bladder syndrome. This means that, unless I’m alone in public toilets, I cannot pee, however badly I need to go. I developed tactics to deal with this, such as loitering outside the gents if I see someone going in, so that I can walk in as they walk out. But if someone follows me in, I find I’m just standing there, which I worry looks odd.

I’m a writer, so am often out and about meeting people in cafes, hotels and at events. My agricultural background means I also meet a lot of my interviewees on farms – but at least there I could pop behind a hedge if I needed to go, and be assured of privacy.

It was while I was doing research for a book on the spiritual connections humans once had with the land that I stumbled across the Christian Naturist Fellowship: a network of people who believe that Christianity and naturism are entirely compatible. Here, I thought, were a community who clearly get closer to nature than most – I was keen to meet them.

One of their committee members, Nigel, suggested I visit his naturist club near Colchester. So one Saturday morning in 2025, I set off to discover what Christian naturists really think and do. He had said that I’d not have to strip off – many don’t on their first visit – but when the time came, that is exactly what I did.

I’d been naked in public once before, but then I’d been one of more than 3,000 people who, in 2016, had stripped off in a Hull city centre park at dawn, daubed themselves with blue body paint, and been photographed by Spencer Tunick as a visual celebration of the city’s relationship with the sea. Then, I’d enjoyed the anonymity of being one in a crowd and, strangely, it still felt as if I was wearing something, albeit just blue paint. Visiting a small naturists’ collective would be different.

After arriving at Springwood Sun Club, Nigel greeted me wearing a warm smile – and a pair of shorts. As it happened, he was not in a rush to shed his clothes either, and we both walked to the clubhouse fully dressed. It could have been any social club, except that the foursome playing miniten outside were in the buff.

articles.title: In praise of the bitter: Alexina Anatole’s recipes for tahini panzanella and curried corn farinata

articles.content:
In Ayurvedic cooking, bitter ingredients are celebrated for their ability to refresh and rebalance. Here, the elegance of tahini and the cleanliness of grapefruit do the heavy lifting

B itterness has long had an image problem: is it delicious or disgusting? Here’s another contradiction: though bitterness seems as if it should sit alongside hot, pungent flavours such as mustard and horseradish, in reality it cools more than it builds. In Ayurvedic cooking, for instance, bitter ingredients are valued for their ability to refresh and rebalance, and those are qualities that run through both of today’s dishes, from the elegant bitterness of tahini in the panzanella to the clean bite of grapefruit in the dipping sauce for the farinata.

500g large tomatoes , eg, beef, oxheart or monterosa 1 tsp flaky sea salt ½ small garlic clove 1 tbsp sherry vinegar , or red-wine vinegar 1 tbsp pomegranate molasses 1 small red onion , peeled and very thinly sliced ½ tbsp capers , finely chopped, or nonpareilles, which are already petite enough ½ tbsp sesame seeds , lightly toasted Basil leaves , to garnish For the croutons 125g sourdough , crusts on, torn into rough pieces 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil ½ tsp flaky sea salt

For the tahini dressing 2 tbsp tahini 1 tbsp lemon juice 1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil ¼ tsp fine sea salt

Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Chop the tomatoes into haphazard, chunky pieces and put them in a colander set over a bowl. Toss with the flaky salt and leave to drain for 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, spread the bread pieces on a baking tray, toss with the olive oil and salt, then bake for 10 minutes, until golden. In a bowl, grate the garlic into the tablespoon of sherry vinegar, to help take the edge off.

Make the tahini dressing by whisking the tahini, lemon juice, olive oil and salt, then gradually add about two tablespoons of ice-cold water until the mix is the consistency of double cream (the amount of water will depend on the thickness of the tahini).

Transfer the drained tomatoes to a serving bowl and stir in the pomegranate molasses, sliced red onion and capers. Add the sherry vinegar and garlic mix, and the croutons, and toss thoroughly. Stir through the tahini dressing, then leave for five to 10 minutes, so the croutons soften a little. Serve garnished with the toasted sesame seeds and basil leaves.

For the farinata 100g chickpea flour ½ tsp ground turmeric ½ tsp garlic powder/granules ½ tsp fine sea salt 1 tsp cumin seeds , toasted 1 tsp coriander seeds , toasted 4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil 75g tinned sweetcorn , drained, or frozen and defrosted 3 spring onions , finely sliced Mint leaves , to serve

For the grapefruit dipping sauce 4 tbsp fresh red grapefruit juice (from about 1 grapefruit) 1 tbsp rice vinegar 1 tsp caster sugar 1 red chilli , finely chopped (seeds and all, if you like things spicy)

In a large jug, combine the chickpea flour, turmeric, garlic powder or granules and salt. Gradually whisk in 230ml cold water, ensuring there are no lumps, then leave to rest for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 230C (210C fan)/450F/gas 8. Roughly crush the cumin and coriander seeds, until broken up but not fully ground.

Place a 20cm nonstick, ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat. Once hot, add three tablespoons of olive oil and leave to heat for a minute. Meanwhile, whisk the last tablespoon of oil into the batter.

Add the crushed spices to the pan, let them sizzle lightly in the oil for 30 seconds, then pour the batter into the centre – it should sizzle. Sprinkle over the corn and spring onions, then bake for 25 minutes, until golden and crisp around the edges. Remove, leave to sit for a minute, then turn out on to a board. Cut into wedges and serve at once with the dipping sauce and mint leaves.

Alexina Anatole is the author of the Small Wins Substack and Sweet: the Secret to the Best Desserts, published by Square Peg at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go to guardianbookshop.com .

articles.content:
Rob Pike was 17 when he and three of his closest friends were in a car that smashed into a tree and split in half. He explains how he coped with the devastation

A fter the car stopped rolling and came to rest on its side, Rob Pike remembers being “hyperfixated” on the rainwater pouring down his face. When he tried to wipe it away with his arm, he realised it wasn’t water. “I look at my arm and it is covered in blood. The next moment, it hit me: oh my gosh, we crashed.”

He was in the back seat next to his best friend, Daniel McCoy. “I look up to my left to see if Daniel’s OK. He’s probably about a foot away from my face and … he’s not OK. I’m looking at my dead best friend and I wish that wasn’t my last memory of him, seeing how broken he was.” They were 17.

“I lost control,” he says. “I am screaming at the top of my lungs. I’m yelling, I’m crying.” Even though he knew that Daniel was dead, he hoped for a miracle. “You spend your life watching Home and Away and Neighbours and you see people getting pulled out of cars and having CPR. If I can scream loud enough, then maybe somebody might come along and save his life.”

A woman had rushed out of her house when she heard the crash and run towards Pike’s screams. She found the car in the bushes. Pike remembers begging her: “‘Please help Daniel. You gotta do something.’ And then she gets down on her hands and knees, in the mud, in the rain, and she looks inside. And I remember her saying: ‘There’s nothing we can do for him. He’s already gone.’

“All of a sudden, I am very aware that I’m trapped in this car. I start freaking out. I’m trying with all my might to pull myself out of this little back window. I’m cutting my hands and I can’t get out.”

The woman stayed with Pike for about 15 minutes, trying to calm him down, until the fire engine and ambulance arrived. “I remember thinking, as soon as they arrived: ‘Everything’s going to be OK.’” The next two weeks are a blank.

Pike grew up in a mining town in the far north-west of Western Australia, with five older half-brothers and half-sisters. He was particularly close to one of his brothers, who taught him to play cricket and football in the back yard. When he was 12, the family moved to Baldivis, a small town about 50km south of Perth.

Life was good. “I was in my final year of high school, I had good friends and I knew what I wanted to do in my life. I had two options: I wanted to go into the Defence Force or I wanted to go and play AFL football for the best AFL football team in Australia, the Fremantle Dockers.” He grins – Fremantle is one of only three AFL teams never to have won a premiership.

On the day of the crash in Baldivis, on 17 August 1999, he was in lessons until lunchtime. His friends Christian Iezzi-Carrello and Adam Stribling, who were a year older and already at university, picked him up from school to go to play golf. “We weren’t any good,” he says. “We just loved getting out there, mucking around, getting in the golf carts – you know, being a little bit silly and having a good time.” McCoy was off sick that day, but Pike was pretty sure he’d want to join them. So he said the words that would later torture him: “Hey, let’s go get Daniel.”

It started to rain, so they went bowling instead. “As much as that day was a horrendous day, I’ll always remember that afternoon and those two games of 10-pin bowling as a fun time with my friends,” he says. “And I’m very grateful for that memory.”

Iezzi-Carrello, the driver, suddenly realised the time. It was nearly 4pm and he had to get to his part-time job at McDonald’s. “So we rushed out of there. We ran out of the building, across the car park, jumped into his car and took off.” It was now pouring with rain. “We were zipping in and out of traffic. We were probably going between 10 and 20 kilometres over the speed limit.” It didn’t cross his mind to object. “At 4.16, everything’s fine. At 4.17, I am the most scared I’ve ever been in my life.”

They were laughing and joking and listening to the radio. Then the car hit a big puddle of water and Iezzi-Carrello lost control. “I can go back to that moment right now,” says Pike. “I can remember closing my eyes and almost in slow motion thinking to myself: this is gonna be bad.” The car aquaplaned, went into a spin, smashed into a tree and split in half.

Pike woke up in Fremantle hospital after a fortnight on life support. At that point, he had no memory of the accident. “I had tubes and cords that were connected to me, keeping me alive. I had one going down my throat and I couldn’t speak. I’m in a back brace, almost like I’m strapped to the bed. I can’t move.”

His father was sitting by his bed. “He must have seen the fear on my face because he grabbed me by the hand. And I remember him saying: ‘Hey, Bob, I’m here.’ I remember that calming me.” His father was silent for a while. “Then he goes to me: ‘Bob, I got to tell you something. Christian, Adam and Daniel have died.’” Iezzi-Carrello and Stribling had been flung out of the car and died on impact.

Pike thought he was dreaming. He started pinching his arm and his chest, hard enough to leave bruises, trying to wake himself. “And I never woke up out of the nightmare. This is real; my friends have gone.”

No one told him the extent of his injuries. He was told he’d had more than 300 stitches and that he’d broken his back. He knew he needed to wear the back brace or risk severing his spinal cord. But he felt cramps and itches in his feet, and he could feel himself wiggling his toes, so he was confident he would eventually walk again.

About four weeks after the accident, he felt an unbearable itch in his foot that he simply had to scratch. “So I’m trying to contort my body to reach down under the blankets. All I feel are bandages. That’s the moment where I’m like: oh my God, what’s this? I rip the blankets off and then, even in this back brace, I sit up, because I need to see. I look down. Now, what I’m expecting to see is two feet and 10 toes. But all I see is bandages where both my legs finish just after my knees. I reckon that was one of the worst moments.” More than half of people who lose a limb experience phantom pains, including itches.

The doctors hadn’t amputated his legs; they had been severed in the crash. When the car hit the tree, the back panel sliced through his legs. “It actually took both my feet. So my feet, still in the shoes, ended up going in the front half of the car, jammed under the front seat, and my body was in the back half of the car.” This panel trapped him inside and saved his life. “It was so tight on my legs that it acted as a tourniquet. Ask any emergency services person: if there is an amputation in a car crash, nine times out of 10, that person dies at the scene because they can’t stop the blood flow.”

His dream of playing for the Dockers was over. “I’m lying in this bed and I’m like: well, that’s not my future any more. You can’t play football because you don’t have feet.”

Over seven weeks in hospital, he had to go through the embarrassment of nurses seeing him naked, bathing him and cleaning him up after he went to the bathroom. “I feel like I’ve lost everything. I’ve lost my friends. I’ve lost my legs. The last thing I had was my dignity and there it goes.”

He cried himself to sleep every night. He had “massive survivor’s guilt” and wished he could exchange his life for one of his friends’. “You almost create this rationale within your own mind: they were a little bit more popular, so less people would be sad if I’d died.” He couldn’t bear the fact that it was his words that had put McCoy in the car. He started making a plan to end his life.

One night, there was a knock at the door of his hospital room. It was McCoy’s parents. He tried to compose himself for their sake, but he couldn’t. “Daniel’s dad puts his arms around me and I bawl my eyes out. He’s saying: ‘It’s gonna be OK, Bob. We’re gonna get through this.’ And I’m thinking to myself: it’s not gonna be OK. I’m not gonna get through this because I’ve checked out. I don’t want to be here any more.

“He grasps me by the shoulders and looks me in the eyes and he goes: ‘Bob, we are so happy that you are alive.’ And those words hit me in my heart.” He knew he couldn’t do anything to add to their pain. He had no choice but to live.

“I remember saying to myself: ‘I can’t give up.’ And I would say it every day, multiple times a day for the first three to four months, over and over.” One day, he realised he’d only had to say it five times instead of 100. Eventually, he didn’t have to say it at all. “I’m not living for them any more,” he realised. “I’m living for me.”

Pike learned to use his prosthetic legs before his stumps had even fully healed; he was determined to walk into his end-of-year school celebration. He started playing cricket again. He got a girlfriend.

To friends, he was the lucky one, the brave one. But he was still full of guilt and very self-conscious about his disability. There were false reports in local newspapers that the boys had been drinking before the crash and that the car was stolen. People would accost him in the street to ask: “What were you guys thinking?” He started self-medicating with alcohol, binge-drinking every weekend to mask “this brokenness within me”. After six months, he finally accepted that he needed therapy.

The other thing that saved him was wheelchair basketball. His dad persuaded him to try it. “I was very ignorant. I’m like: a bunch of disabled people playing basketball?” He went to a game and was “blown away. What I’m watching is athletes flying around this court, hitting each other, smacking each other. And I’m like: yes, this is awesome!”

It helped fill the gap left by football and he loved the physicality of it. “No one was like: I can’t hit you because you’ve got no legs.” He threw himself into the sport and ended up playing for Perth Wheelcats and Australia, then moved to Spain for a couple of years to play professionally. Today, he is the head coach of the Wombats, the Australian women’s 3x3 wheelchair basketball team. We meet in Glasgow on the opening day of the Commonwealth Games; they will go on to take the bronze medal.

Pike, 44, is married with two children. He is proud to be on the board of the Paraplegic Benefit Fund of Australia, which supports people with spinal cord injuries, and to do road safety advocacy. Reliving the worst day of his life is tough, but it helps give his friends’ deaths meaning. “I can share it with 16-, 17-year-old students and hopefully inspire them to be better drivers, but also better people.” He says that he is a “nicer, more empathetic” person since the accident.

He still has setbacks. During Covid, more than 20 years after the crash, he woke up with “extreme panic attacks”. All he could think was: “I’ve gotta get out.” He slept outside on garden furniture for two weeks, then took off the window in the front room and slept on a recliner for a month. He had another panic attack when he was driving. “I remember feeling: oh my gosh, I’m trapped to my legs and I’m trapped in this car. And then – it’s strange how the mind works – I actually feel like I’m trapped in this world.” He saw a tree and, for a split second, it seemed like a way out. That was when he knew he needed to see a psychiatrist again.

“You think you’re done,” he says, referring to his initial therapy after the crash. “But what the psych said to me is that your body protects itself. And then when it feels like it’s in a safer space, things start to come to the surface, which was my trauma of being stuck in the car.” Now, he says, “I’ve come through the other side. And I feel like I’m a pretty complete, whole person, and I’m in a really positive place.”

Life still throws curveballs. Towards the end of our conversation, he casually mentions that he had a heart attack three months ago. He thought he’d pulled a muscle; he ended up “going into complete heart failure” and being hospitalised for 12 days. It turned out he has hereditary high cholesterol – his dad had a heart attack in his early 50s. “I thought I could just be healthier and eat well and go to the gym. I learned the hard way that it doesn’t matter how fit you are. If your cholesterol is an issue, it’s an issue.”

These days, he believes in counting his blessings. “It’s very easy to look at what you don’t have. We should be looking at what we do have. I don’t think we’re called to just sit there and exist and wait till the end. I think we’re called to go out there and live life and be kind and be the best person we can.”

He was in the back seat next to his best friend, Daniel McCoy. “I look up to my left to see if Daniel’s OK. He’s probably about a foot away from my face and … he’s not OK. I’m looking at my dead best friend and I wish that wasn’t my last memory of him, seeing how broken he was.” They were 17.

“I lost control,” he says. “I am screaming at the top of my lungs. I’m yelling, I’m crying.” Even though he knew that Daniel was dead, he hoped for a miracle. “You spend your life watching Home and Away and Neighbours and you see people getting pulled out of cars and having CPR. If I can scream loud enough, then maybe somebody might come along and save his life.”

A woman had rushed out of her house when she heard the crash and run towards Pike’s screams. She found the car in the bushes. Pike remembers begging her: “‘Please help Daniel. You gotta do something.’ And then she gets down on her hands and knees, in the mud, in the rain, and she looks inside. And I remember her saying: ‘There’s nothing we can do for him. He’s already gone.’

“All of a sudden, I am very aware that I’m trapped in this car. I start freaking out. I’m trying with all my might to pull myself out of this little back window. I’m cutting my hands and I can’t get out.”

The woman stayed with Pike for about 15 minutes, trying to calm him down, until the fire engine and ambulance arrived. “I remember thinking, as soon as they arrived: ‘Everything’s going to be OK.’” The next two weeks are a blank.

Pike grew up in a mining town in the far north-west of Western Australia, with five older half-brothers and half-sisters. He was particularly close to one of his brothers, who taught him to play cricket and football in the back yard. When he was 12, the family moved to Baldivis, a small town about 50km south of Perth.

Life was good. “I was in my final year of high school, I had good friends and I knew what I wanted to do in my life. I had two options: I wanted to go into the Defence Force or I wanted to go and play AFL football for the best AFL football team in Australia, the Fremantle Dockers.” He grins – Fremantle is one of only three AFL teams never to have won a premiership.

On the day of the crash in Baldivis, on 17 August 1999, he was in lessons until lunchtime. His friends Christian Iezzi-Carrello and Adam Stribling, who were a year older and already at university, picked him up from school to go to play golf. “We weren’t any good,” he says. “We just loved getting out there, mucking around, getting in the golf carts – you know, being a little bit silly and having a good time.” McCoy was off sick that day, but Pike was pretty sure he’d want to join them. So he said the words that would later torture him: “Hey, let’s go get Daniel.”

It started to rain, so they went bowling instead. “As much as that day was a horrendous day, I’ll always remember that afternoon and those two games of 10-pin bowling as a fun time with my friends,” he says. “And I’m very grateful for that memory.”

Iezzi-Carrello, the driver, suddenly realised the time. It was nearly 4pm and he had to get to his part-time job at McDonald’s. “So we rushed out of there. We ran out of the building, across the car park, jumped into his car and took off.” It was now pouring with rain. “We were zipping in and out of traffic. We were probably going between 10 and 20 kilometres over the speed limit.” It didn’t cross his mind to object. “At 4.16, everything’s fine. At 4.17, I am the most scared I’ve ever been in my life.”

They were laughing and joking and listening to the radio. Then the car hit a big puddle of water and Iezzi-Carrello lost control. “I can go back to that moment right now,” says Pike. “I can remember closing my eyes and almost in slow motion thinking to myself: this is gonna be bad.” The car aquaplaned, went into a spin, smashed into a tree and split in half.

Pike woke up in Fremantle hospital after a fortnight on life support. At that point, he had no memory of the accident. “I had tubes and cords that were connected to me, keeping me alive. I had one going down my throat and I couldn’t speak. I’m in a back brace, almost like I’m strapped to the bed. I can’t move.”

His father was sitting by his bed. “He must have seen the fear on my face because he grabbed me by the hand. And I remember him saying: ‘Hey, Bob, I’m here.’ I remember that calming me.” His father was silent for a while. “Then he goes to me: ‘Bob, I got to tell you something. Christian, Adam and Daniel have died.’” Iezzi-Carrello and Stribling had been flung out of the car and died on impact.

Pike thought he was dreaming. He started pinching his arm and his chest, hard enough to leave bruises, trying to wake himself. “And I never woke up out of the nightmare. This is real; my friends have gone.”

No one told him the extent of his injuries. He was told he’d had more than 300 stitches and that he’d broken his back. He knew he needed to wear the back brace or risk severing his spinal cord. But he felt cramps and itches in his feet, and he could feel himself wiggling his toes, so he was confident he would eventually walk again.

About four weeks after the accident, he felt an unbearable itch in his foot that he simply had to scratch. “So I’m trying to contort my body to reach down under the blankets. All I feel are bandages. That’s the moment where I’m like: oh my God, what’s this? I rip the blankets off and then, even in this back brace, I sit up, because I need to see. I look down. Now, what I’m expecting to see is two feet and 10 toes. But all I see is bandages where both my legs finish just after my knees. I reckon that was one of the worst moments.” More than half of people who lose a limb experience phantom pains, including itches.

The doctors hadn’t amputated his legs; they had been severed in the crash. When the car hit the tree, the back panel sliced through his legs. “It actually took both my feet. So my feet, still in the shoes, ended up going in the front half of the car, jammed under the front seat, and my body was in the back half of the car.” This panel trapped him inside and saved his life. “It was so tight on my legs that it acted as a tourniquet. Ask any emergency services person: if there is an amputation in a car crash, nine times out of 10, that person dies at the scene because they can’t stop the blood flow.”
His dream of playing for the Dockers was over. “I’m lying in this bed and I’m like: well, that’s not my future any more. You can’t play football because you don’t have feet.”

Over seven weeks in hospital, he had to go through the embarrassment of nurses seeing him naked, bathing him and cleaning him up after he went to the bathroom. “I feel like I’ve lost everything. I’ve lost my friends. I’ve lost my legs. The last thing I had was my dignity and there it goes.”

He cried himself to sleep every night. He had “massive survivor’s guilt” and wished he could exchange his life for one of his friends’. “You almost create this rationale within your own mind: they were a little bit more popular, so less people would be sad if I’d died.” He couldn’t bear the fact that it was his words that had put McCoy in the car. He started making a plan to end his life.

One night, there was a knock at the door of his hospital room. It was McCoy’s parents. He tried to compose himself for their sake, but he couldn’t. “Daniel’s dad puts his arms around me and I bawl my eyes out. He’s saying: ‘It’s gonna be OK, Bob. We’re gonna get through this.’ And I’m thinking to myself: it’s not gonna be OK. I’m not gonna get through this because I’ve checked out. I don’t want to be here any more.

“He grasps me by the shoulders and looks me in the eyes and he goes: ‘Bob, we are so happy that you are alive.’ And those words hit me in my heart.” He knew he couldn’t do anything to add to their pain. He had no choice but to live.

“I remember saying to myself: ‘I can’t give up.’ And I would say it every day, multiple times a day for the first three to four months, over and over.” One day, he realised he’d only had to say it five times instead of 100. Eventually, he didn’t have to say it at all. “I’m not living for them any more,” he realised. “I’m living for me.”

Pike learned to use his prosthetic legs before his stumps had even fully healed; he was determined to walk into his end-of-year school celebration. He started playing cricket again. He got a girlfriend.

To friends, he was the lucky one, the brave one. But he was still full of guilt and very self-conscious about his disability. There were false reports in local newspapers that the boys had been drinking before the crash and that the car was stolen. People would accost him in the street to ask: “What were you guys thinking?” He started self-medicating with alcohol, binge-drinking every weekend to mask “this brokenness within me”. After six months, he finally accepted that he needed therapy.

The other thing that saved him was wheelchair basketball. His dad persuaded him to try it. “I was very ignorant. I’m like: a bunch of disabled people playing basketball?” He went to a game and was “blown away. What I’m watching is athletes flying around this court, hitting each other, smacking each other. And I’m like: yes, this is awesome!”

It helped fill the gap left by football and he loved the physicality of it. “No one was like: I can’t hit you because you’ve got no legs.” He threw himself into the sport and ended up playing for Perth Wheelcats and Australia, then moved to Spain for a couple of years to play professionally. Today, he is the head coach of the Wombats, the Australian women’s 3x3 wheelchair basketball team. We meet in Glasgow on the opening day of the Commonwealth Games; they will go on to take the bronze medal.

Pike, 44, is married with two children. He is proud to be on the board of the Paraplegic Benefit Fund of Australia, which supports people with spinal cord injuries, and to do road safety advocacy. Reliving the worst day of his life is tough, but it helps give his friends’ deaths meaning. “I can share it with 16-, 17-year-old students and hopefully inspire them to be better drivers, but also better people.” He says that he is a “nicer, more empathetic” person since the accident.

He still has setbacks. During Covid, more than 20 years after the crash, he woke up with “extreme panic attacks”. All he could think was: “I’ve gotta get out.” He slept outside on garden furniture for two weeks, then took off the window in the front room and slept on a recliner for a month. He had another panic attack when he was driving. “I remember feeling: oh my gosh, I’m trapped to my legs and I’m trapped in this car. And then – it’s strange how the mind works – I actually feel like I’m trapped in this world.” He saw a tree and, for a split second, it seemed like a way out. That was when he knew he needed to see a psychiatrist again.

“You think you’re done,” he says, referring to his initial therapy after the crash. “But what the psych said to me is that your body protects itself. And then when it feels like it’s in a safer space, things start to come to the surface, which was my trauma of being stuck in the car.” Now, he says, “I’ve come through the other side. And I feel like I’m a pretty complete, whole person, and I’m in a really positive place.”

Life still throws curveballs. Towards the end of our conversation, he casually mentions that he had a heart attack three months ago. He thought he’d pulled a muscle; he ended up “going into complete heart failure” and being hospitalised for 12 days. It turned out he has hereditary high cholesterol – his dad had a heart attack in his early 50s. “I thought I could just be healthier and eat well and go to the gym. I learned the hard way that it doesn’t matter how fit you are. If your cholesterol is an issue, it’s an issue.”

These days, he believes in counting his blessings. “It’s very easy to look at what you don’t have. We should be looking at what we do have. I don’t think we’re called to just sit there and exist and wait till the end. I think we’re called to go out there and live life and be kind and be the best person we can.”

articles.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
articles.summary: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study. Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems

Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.

Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.

More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa , followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.

On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.

Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.

“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.

The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.

Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.

“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”

The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.

The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.

The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.

The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.

While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades .

“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.

The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.

It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.

Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

articles.title: Championship roundup: West Ham go top after Bowen double sinks Bolton
articles.summary: England forward scores twice in 3-2 victory Southampton 3-1 Swansea; Watford 2-1 Preston Captain Jarrod Bowen scored twice as West Ham ’s 3-2 win over Bolton took them top of the Championship on goal difference. The England international opened the scoring after 13 minutes and earned his side a first win at Bolton for 31 years with his second 13 minutes from time. In between, Wanderers, beaten for a fourth successive outing, equalised through midfielder Ethan Erhahon’s maiden goal for the club and they looked on course for a ninth successive league victory over the Hammers when Ruben Rodrigues converted a 27th-minute penalty. Instead, Konstantinos Mavropanos levelled with a 31st-minute header and Bowen completed the comeback. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Captain Jarrod Bowen scored twice as West Ham ’s 3-2 win over Bolton took them top of the Championship on goal difference. The England international opened the scoring after 13 minutes and earned his side a first win at Bolton for 31 years with his second 13 minutes from time.

In between, Wanderers, beaten for a fourth successive outing, equalised through midfielder Ethan Erhahon’s maiden goal for the club and they looked on course for a ninth successive league victory over the Hammers when Ruben Rodrigues converted a 27th-minute penalty. Instead, Konstantinos Mavropanos levelled with a 31st-minute header and Bowen completed the comeback.

Cyle Larin scored his fifth goal of the season as Southampton beat Swansea 3-1 to beat the side who were top of the table for the second home match in a row. Larin, who is the joint-top scorer in the Championship, found the net either side of Finn Azaz and Leo Scienza strikes to make it 13 games unbeaten at St Mary’s.

Watford shook off an awful first-half display to grab a 2-1 victory over Preston , who suffered their fifth defeat in six league games. Callum Lang had put the visitors ahead in the sixth minute as they threatened to overrun the Hornets, who hit back with two second-half goals in seven minutes from Edo Kayembe and Mamadou Doumbia.

Wrexham ’s wait for a home win goes on after they were held to a 1-1 draw by winless Burnley who sit one place off the bottom of the table. Jacques Ekomie headed in his second goal for the club since joining in a £7m deal from Angers, cancelling out Zeki Amdouni’s first-half effort for the Clarets who at least ended a run of seven straight away defeats dating back to last term.

But it was a result that does little to help either side in their pursuit of promotion, with Wrexham having lost the momentum they carried into last season while Burnley face bigger problems after relegation from the top flight, having won only one league game since October. Former England striker Jamie Vardy joined this week, but the 39-year-old was suspended for this match as a result of yellow cards collected during his time with Italian side Cremonese.

Sheffield United returned to winning ways after a display of ruthless finishing secured a 2-1 win at Blackburn . All the goals came in a first half that Rovers dominated and deservedly took the lead in through Kristi Montgomery’s first goal for the club on 20 minutes. The Blades turned the game on its head with goals from their only two shots of the half as Tom Cannon stroked home a second on this ground in two weeks in the 35th minute. Sydie Peck rifled home his first of the season a minute before the break to complete the turnaround.

Cardiff ’s winless start to the season continued as Stoke held on for a 1-1 draw in the Welsh capital and their first away point since January. Stoke had hope of an away-day success after a run of nine straight Championship defeats when Ben Johnson scored midway through the first half. But the Potters came under fierce pressure in the second half and Joel Colwill’s headed home for Cardiff hosts who hit a post three times. The draw – Cardiff’s fourth in six games – was enough to take the home side out of the relegation zone, while Stoke slip to 15th.

articles.title: Company review – Casey Affleck entertains us with creepy campfire tales
articles.summary: Venice film festival: Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged men Gather ye ’round the glowing screen for a Casey Affleck campfire tale. It contains superstitions and murder and human oddities of all stripes. An old hermit in his shack. Something nasty in the woodshed. If you like the first tale, fill your boots, settle back, because here comes another and another; each sparked by the embers of its neighbour and playing out with the same deliberately theatrical panache. Affleck’s picture roams and rambles like a creepy cracker-barrel Jackanory. Actually there is much to relish in Company, Affleck’s third film as a director, even if many of its elements feel like off-the-peg eccentricities; a little too laundered and self-consciously strange. It begins in tried and tested fashion with the arrival of a mysterious stranger on a dark winter’s night. The stranger takes a seat and spins a tale, at which point December 1975 melts into 1953, then 1903, before finally the film crosses the ocean to Europe at the tail end of the plague. Venice film festival: Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged men

G ather ye ’round the glowing screen for a Casey Affleck campfire tale. It contains superstitions and murder and human oddities of all stripes. An old hermit in his shack. Something nasty in the woodshed. If you like the first tale, fill your boots, settle back, because here comes another and another; each sparked by the embers of its neighbour and playing out with the same deliberately theatrical panache. Affleck’s picture roams and rambles like a creepy cracker-barrel Jackanory.

Actually there is much to relish in Company, Affleck’s third film as a director, even if many of its elements feel like off-the-peg eccentricities; a little too laundered and self-consciously strange. It begins in tried and tested fashion with the arrival of a mysterious stranger on a dark winter’s night. The stranger takes a seat and spins a tale, at which point December 1975 melts into 1953, then 1903, before finally the film crosses the ocean to Europe at the tail end of the plague. Nick Nolte is a hermit pining for his lost daughter, while Ben Mendelsohn plays a mean, mordant farmer who reaches for his handgun too readily. Both men, one suspects, are destined for a bloody end.

Where is it leading, this tale of a woman who tells a tale of a woman? Into the woods and through the darkness, of course, although the film’s centrepiece story, set in the Rockies at the turn of the 20th century, provides a torch to dimly light our way. Here Adelaide Clemens and Scoot McNairy play Rebecca and Emmett, a hard-bitten farming couple who discover a teenage boy, Caleb, lying prostrate in the snow. Caleb is played by Atticus Affleck, the director’s youngest son, with a vulpine gaucheness which grows more assured and compelling the longer he’s on screen. Caleb tells Rebecca that he is much older than he looks; that he’s been “hither and yon” and visited Argentina and London. When she starts to suspect the boy may be behind a spate of grisly local killings, Caleb’s bleak pronouncements seem hardly designed to dissuade her. “This whole world is tall grass,” he explains. “You have no idea of the dangers underfoot.”

Affleck co-scripted Company alongside Ron Hansen, the author of The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, which was made into a fabulous 2007 film by Andrew Dominik. Affleck co-starred as Ford, a snivelling beta male with dark dreams of glory, unsure whether he wants to befriend or kill his idol, and there is a similar scary ambivalence to the character of Caleb, who settles in at the farm and appears in no hurry to leave. Caleb might be a fantasist, bumming for work in the mountains. He might be a demon, blown in from the backwoods or beyond.

As for Affleck, his career has peaked and troughed since those heady days of Jesse James. He won the best actor Oscar for Manchester by the Sea and cropped up as an army intelligence man in Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer. Off-screen, though, he has been dogged by accusations of sexual harassment ( subsequently settled out of court ) and it is perhaps no coincidence that his passion project is occasionally afflicted by pangs of self-pity and features men who have been wronged and weren’t believed by their peers. The hermit’s wife was killed by an errant, unrepentant physician. Emmett witnessed his father shot dead by a well-connected landowner. The law is a joke; the innocent are kicked to the curb. But these jarring asides stray too close to special pleading. They add little to the narrative; he could have easily cut them out.

Company is better – more satisfying – when it circles back to the fire and picks up the main thread; when it is sticking most closely to reliable American Gothic tropes. Affleck clearly loves this dark sub-genre and elects to play it straight, and his enthusiasm is infectious and embeds us in the yarn. His film is a diversion. Maybe it doesn’t wholly add up. But it contains a ripe gamey flavour with a crunch of buckshot in every bite. Don’t step into the woods after dark, it advises. And if a mysterious stranger taps at your door before dinner, think very carefully before introducing them to your guests.

articles.title: South Park changes name to South America in response to Trump changes
articles.summary: Satirical program’s new title is ‘inspired by bravery and patriotism’ of Apple and Google, who capitulated to Trump’s requests to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ In light of Donald Trump ’s attempts to rename a gulf, lakes and even states after “America”, South Park , the animated satirical program that has long skewered those in power, has announced an official name change. The 29th season of “South America” will premiere on 16 September, and stream globally on Paramount+. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Satirical program’s new title is ‘inspired by bravery and patriotism’ of Apple and Google, who capitulated to Trump’s requests to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’

In light of Donald Trump ’s attempts to rename a gulf, lakes and even states after “America”, South Park , the animated satirical program that has long skewered those in power, has announced an official name change. For its 29th season, the Comedy Central series will be known as “South America”.

“Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA,” creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker said in a statement. “We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount – a Skydance Capitulation.” The show’s parent company, Paramount Skydance, owned by Trump ally David Ellison, is poised to become one of the biggest media conglomerates in the US after the Trump administration approved its $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery (WBD), drawing much creative industry backlash .

The tongue-in-cheek news comes a day after the US president suggested on social media that the state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America” with an AI-generated video that depicted him placing the word “America” over “Mexico” on a “welcome to New Mexico” sign. (The US federal government has no authority to change a state’s name.) The post drew swift condemnation from Democrats, who accused him of trying to distract from his war in Iran and rising prices.

The renaming brouhaha is now a standard Trump move , dating back to the early hours of his second term, when he moved to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”. Last month, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, the administration tried to do the same with Lake Ontario, pushing to relabel it “Lake America”.

The Emmy-winning, gleefully offensive comedy series, which first aired in 1997, has long been a thorn in the Trump administration’s side, as one of the few programs to successfully ridicule and ambitiously poke at an administration often resistant to satire . Creators Parker and Stone have repeatedly drawn ire from Trump and other Maga figures for, among other things, depicting Trump naked in bed with Satan , showing an animated Trump with small genitalia and portraying former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem as a puppy killer whose Botoxed face occasionally melts off.

In August, a writer for the show announced that he purchased the rights to trumpkennedycenter.org, predicting that Trump would change the name of the Kennedy Center after he purged the leadership of the arts institution, installed himself as chair and stocked the board with loyalists .

The 29th season of “South America” will premiere on 16 September, and stream globally on Paramount+.

articles.content:
When Phoebe Bridgers appeared at Venice international film festival with unshaven legs this weekend, it shouldn’t have made headlines – but did. What do young women make of the current expectations around depilation?

I n 2026, female body hair feels as if it should be the least of anyone’s concerns. But although we may think we’ve come a long way since Julia Roberts’ unshaven underarm caused a furore at the 1999 London premiere of Notting Hill, depilation remains a staple of many women’s grooming routines – and when singer turned actor Phoebe Bridgers made her Venice film festival debut last weekend, her unshaven legs still made headlines.

Even so, her au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations. Vogue decreed that “rather than undermining the femininity of the look, unapologetic hair sharpened it”, and pictures of the 32-year-old’s hair-covered calves were generally praised by fans. But what do other gen Z and millennial women make of the decision to ditch the razor?

“Hell yeah!” is 27-year-old PhD student Anna Busuttil’s response. “I think it’s awesome; cool and rebellious,” she says – a view that chimes with that of most of the women I speak to outside University College London’s Bloomsbury campus. Busuttil says she sees a lot more women nowadays choosing not to remove their body hair. “I know people who dye their armpit hair a certain colour as well, so it stands out even more. I feel like leg hair is more taboo for women; it feels like such a ‘masculine’ thing, and legs are supposed to be a really sexy part of a woman.”

Francesca Hall, 25, agrees: she removes her leg hair, but doesn’t worry about her underarms. Yet she feels that, if anything, it’s becoming less common to go unshaven. “There’s been a general shift, culturally, towards more conservative ideas,” says the student union-worker. “It’s the same with veganism; it’s gone backwards a bit. My friendship group is quite queer, leftwing, and not everyone would remove their leg hair.” But, she says, not removing leg hair is more common “in those circles … I definitely think there’s a correlation there.”

“I’ve got really hairy legs!” says student Phoebe Green, 21, hitching up her long shorts so I can get a better look. “I don’t really pay attention to the trends that are going around; having leg hair doesn’t affect my life in any way,” she says. “I’ve definitely had a few comments, a few condescending dudes being like, ‘why aren’t they shaved?’ But I get a lot of compliments from girls, there’s a lot of solidarity.”

Children’s nurse Venus Whyte, 23, thinks that attitudes are changing among younger generations – albeit slowly. “I think society puts pressure on women to shave when they don’t really want to,” she says. “If I’m wearing something where my legs are showing, I would prefer to shave but that’s just what I feel comfortable doing.”

Not everyone thinks that leg hair remains the most taboo type of female body hair: for 24-year-old Wendi Fei, it’s armpit hair. She will shave hers for the first time ever this week, for her graduation ceremony. “It’s a formal event so I will be wearing a dress,” she explains. “I don’t think women really need to shave – men don’t need to do it – but some women think that it’s not beautiful.”

Bridgers was also at a formal event: she paired her unshaven calves with a Gucci skirt suit at the photocall for her first acting role, in A24’s psychological crime thriller Primetime. Online, Bridgers fans – or “ Pharbs ” – appeared to approve: “Sorry I actually might cry this is the first time I’ve seen a favourite artist of mine with her leg hair out while wearing feminine clothing like it’s the most normal thing in the world (which it should be!!)” wrote X user @starforthemagic ; “wait this is literally so rare for public figures omg …. queen” agreed @yyelyahkwonn .

But for 22-year-old student Matilda Moore, social media can sometimes be part of why women feel required to conform to certain beauty standards. “Women shouldn’t have to worry about removing body hair – it’s down to individual preference,” she says, “but I still see, sadly, on social media, that women can get a lot of backlash for how they present themselves, which I think is unfair.”

Postgrad student Sarah Cender, 26, agrees that while many of her friends would be happy not to remove their body hair, they worry about how they might be seen by their peers. “I don’t think that it matters – but other people might judge you or see you differently,” she says. Laser hair removal has become more common than shaving or waxing among her friendship group: “so you can just get rid of the hair permanently”.

“I have lots of friends who religiously get laser everywhere,” agrees Hannah, a legal and corporate services manager at a trend forecasting company, “but I can’t even be bothered plucking my eyebrows, you know?” The 30-year-old feels that, today, people are more empowered to do what they want when it comes to grooming, especially compared with when she was younger. “I am just pretty lazy, I’ll be honest,” she laughs.

articles.title: New law to force tech firms to stop children taking or sharing nude images
articles.summary: The government said it will legislate "as soon as they can" but may "reassess" its plans if firms make the desired changes sooner.
articles.content:
The government has said it will introduce a new law to force tech firms to prevent children from taking or sharing nude images on mobile devices.

Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, were given three months in June to block access to nude images on smartphones and other devices used by under-18s.

But culture secretary Lisa Nandy MP told MPs on Tuesday that despite "significant commitments" from both companies, current proposals "do not meet the scale of this crisis".

She said ministers would look to legislate "as soon as they can" - with the caveat it may reassess these if firms develop and implement solutions sooner.

Alongside making tech firms block nudity on devices used by children at device-level, the government said its draft legislation would also make providers of apps used by children introduce similar blocks on nude imagery.

"This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world," Nandy said.

She told MPs that Apple and Google had already made "meaningful changes" to block nudity on smartphones used by children at the core of their systems, but more action was needed.

An Apple spokesperson said it launched its Communication Safety feature in 2021 to help stop children from seeing or sharing imagery containing nudity - and had since "continued to expand its capabilities".

"We share the UK's commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe," they said.

A Google spokesperson told the BBC it was an "industry leader in combating non-consensual intimate imagery and advancing child safety across our products".

They added Google was pleased to have "made progress" and remained committed to working on efforts to keep children safe online.

The government proposals have been welcomed by organisations and charities calling for tougher measures and technical solutions to stop children from not just seeing, but also capturing and sharing nudity on smartphones.

Ofcom data suggests that a growing proportion of younger children in the UK own a smartphone - and that the number of those do increases with age.
